title: On economy, Vance says "we're turning the ship around"
summary: As Americans express frustration with the country's economic outlook, Vice President JD Vance told CBS News this week it could take some time to see improvement.
story: As Americans express frustration with the country's economic outlook, Vice President JD Vance told CBS News this week it could take some time to see improvement.

"I'll be the first person to tell you that just as this country wasn't broken in one presidential term, it's gonna take more than 18 months to fix things and turn them around," Vance said during a town hall in Michigan that aired Saturday evening.

Vance was responding to a question from a woman who said her small business is struggling. Polls show that most Americans are dissatisfied with the state of the economy and frustrated with inflation, and the majority of voters blame the Trump administration's policies.
President Trump is more positive, giving his administration an "A+" on the economy.

Asked about Mr. Trump's characterization of the economy by "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil, Vance said: "I think that what the president is saying is that we are seeing all of these massive new investments come into our country. But he would be the first person to tell you that you gotta build the factories first, before you can employ the workers working in those factories."
"I think what we're doing is, we're turning the ship around," the vice president continued.

summary: Vice President JD Vance told CBS News in a "Things That Matter" town hall in Michigan that anybody who is "selling access to the White House" should "suffer consequences."
story: Vice President JD Vance told CBS News that anybody who is "selling access to the White House" should "suffer consequences."
Vance spoke with "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil during a one-hour town hall in Michigan that aired on Saturday evening, less than three weeks before the midterm elections.

Dokoupil pointed to a string of recent reports, including Mr. Trump's staggering cryptocurrency earnings, and the ousting of U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle over allegations she asked a man who was seeking help from the Trump administration to wire her $100,000.
"First of all, if somebody's selling access to the White House, that's disgusting and despicable and they should suffer consequences," Vance responded.
He went on to say, "I want to make those judgments based on the facts and not based on a random news media report that I read."
Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing. Mr. Trump has denied any conflicts of interest.

Congressional Democrats have vowed to investigate the Trump administration if they win control of the House or Senate, which would grant them control over committees and allow them to issue subpoenas to administration officials.
Asked if the administration would comply with any subpoenas, Vance said: "Of course I will. Look, I mean, we follow the law."

title: Vance says admin. must take action when ICE agents "screw up"
summary: Vice President JD Vance acknowledged that there are some federal immigration officers "who really screw up."
story: Washington — Vice President JD Vance acknowledged that there are some federal immigration officers "who really screw up" and said the Trump administration has a responsibility to take action against those who do.

Vance sat down with "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil for a one-hour town hall in Michigan, which aired Saturday. Michigan is home to one of the closely watched Senate races between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.
During an exchange about immigration, Vance drew comparisons between law enforcement officers and members of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE.

"Most of them are amazing people who are patriots and they wanna do a good job protecting their country. Sometimes you have some people who make mistakes. Sometimes you have some people who really screw up," Vance said. "And obviously, we have a responsibility to prosecute, investigate when people do screw up."

Dokoupil pressed the vice president on some of those instances, noting that in some cases, "people talk about them before they're investigated," and he asked Vance about the biggest mistakes involving ICE's immigration actions. Vance declined to single out any incidents but said the Trump administration has responded when officers have been accused of misconduct.

"There are a number of cases where we've investigated and either provided further training, or sometimes even provided disciplinary situations within ICE," the vice president said. "We don't always advertise that stuff, as you know, Tony, because we believe that people have to be judged in a court of law and through a normal investigatory process."

Since the Trump administration has ramped up immigration enforcement actions as part of President Trump's immigration crackdown, officers with ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Protection have come under criticism for their use-of-force practices.

Two Americans, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were shot and killed by immigration authorities during protests in Minnesota earlier this year. The ICE officer who fatally shot Good, Jonathan Ross, was placed on administrative leave shortly after the shooting. In May, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul questioned whether Ross had been reassigned to her state. The Department of Homeland Security declined to say at the time where Ross was working.
No criminal charges have been filed in either case. The Justice Department opened an investigation into Pretti's shooting earlier this year.
There have since been a series of incidents involving immigration officers during targeted enforcement operations.
An ICE officer in May fatally shot a 25-year-old Colombian man in his car in Maine in July, and in September, an immigration officer shot a Venezuelan man in the back in Austin, Texas.

Earlier this month, ICE agents shot a man in New York during a targeted enforcement operation, striking him in the neck. The agents were trying to arrest the man, Oscar Belgal, who is from the Dominican Republic, with a 5-year-old boy in the back seat.
Then, a vehicle driven by ICE agents hit and injured a man near Houston.

title: Feds probing suspicious letters to election officials, lawmakers
summary: Federal investigators said they are looking into suspicious letters containing unknown substances that were mailed to state election officials and congressional offices.
story: Washington — Federal investigators said Thursday that they are looking into "suspicious" letters mailed to state election officials and congressional offices, some of which contained unknown substances.

At least seven Democratic Senate offices and two House members' offices were sent the letters, most of which were intercepted before they were delivered. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's office was one of those targeted, CBS News has learned. At least two Senate Republicans were also sent letters on Friday.

The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating the "suspicious mailings," according to Brendan Donahue, the deputy chief inspector at the USPIS. Donahue told reporters earlier in the day that some letters have contained an unknown substance and that they were sent to "various addresses nationwide," including "secretary of state offices and the related election offices."

"We are committed to protecting our nation's election officials from threatening and dangerous mail. Any threat or attack on an election official is unacceptable," Donahue said. "Our partners, including the FBI and we at the Postal Inspection Service, will bring all of our resources to bear on these investigations."

The Senate sergeant at arms also issued a notice to congressional staff informing them of the investigation. The message, which was obtained by CBS News, said congressional offices were among those who received the suspicious letters.

Democratic Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia on Saturday confirmed the FBI contacted his office to report that investigators had intercepted mail containing a suspicious substance addressed to his district office.
"I am grateful to law enforcement for their efforts to keep my staff safe. Threats and attempts at intimidation are unacceptable and must not be tolerated," Scott said on social media.

A spokesperson for Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester told CBS News that a state office received a suspicious letter that contained a white powder. The letter was not opened in the office, the spokesperson said.

A letter meant for New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand was found at the senator's office in New York City and postal inspectors were on the scene to investigate, an aide for the senator said. A letter intended for one of Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks' former state office was intercepted by the Postal Service, her office said Friday.

Six workers in Democratic Rep. Ritchie Torres' office in the Bronx were exposed to a white powder found in a letter on Friday. The substance was determined to be harmless. Torres said the address on the envelope indicated it was from San Antonio, Texas, and his team has turned it over to the FBI for further investigation.
A spokesman for Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut also said his office was "sent a letter with a suspicious substance."

"Our office was promptly informed of the letter by FBI, SAA, and Capitol Police, and we continue to work closely with them and federal law enforcement," said Josh Sorbe, a spokesman for Murphy. "Due to those efforts and various safety protocols, the Senator and staff were not in immediate danger."
A letter was also sent to Sen. Alex Padilla's office, according to a spokesperson for the California Democrat.
"We received the notification from the FBI that one of our offices was mailed a letter containing a suspicious substance, but it was intercepted by USPS," the spokesperson said.
A suspicious letter was sent to the office of Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware, according to a spokesperson, who said the office was "working with law enforcement."
On Friday, Republican Sens. Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Pete Ricketts of Nebraska reported receiving suspicious letters.

Ricketts said his office in Omaha was sent a letter with a "powdery substance" that matched the description of other suspicious packages, and law enforcement "confirmed the substance was not harmful."
Rounds said his office in Sioux Falls was evacuated after it received suspicious mail.

The House sergeant at arms sent a notice to the lower chamber's offices on Thursday stating that no House members were known to have been targeted, a message that came before the discovery of powder at Torres' office.

Federal officials are working to identify the responsible parties and have intercepted some of the letters, Donahue said. Donahue declined to provide an exact number of incidents or discuss possible connections, citing the ongoing investigation. He added that investigators would bring their full resources to bear on the cases.
The development comes less than three weeks before the midterm elections. Federal investigators also probed a series of suspicious letters ahead of the 2024 elections.
In addition to the congressional offices, top election officials in at least eight states have reported that their offices were sent suspicious packages in recent days.

Delaware's Department of Elections said in a post on X that it "received and opened a letter which was discovered to contain a white powdery substance" on Thursday. "Staff members followed security and USPS instructions on handling suspicious mail," the post said.
Louisiana Secretary of State Nancy Landry said Tuesday that an employee in her office's Elections Division opened a package and found a white powder.
"Law enforcement responded to today's incident and conducted tests that found no evidence of harmful substances," she wrote on Facebook, adding that no one was injured.
The Oklahoma State Election Board said it received an envelope containing "suspicious" white powder Tuesday morning, and its office was evacuated.
Paul Ziriax, secretary of the election board, said no one was hurt as a result of the incident, and law enforcement is investigating.
The Wisconsin Elections Commission said it received a "suspicious mail piece" on Wednesday, but "field testing confirmed no hazardous material was detected."

The secretaries of state in Pennsylvania, Maryland, New Hampshire, Ohio and Mississippi said their offices were also sent suspicious mail, but the deliveries were intercepted by the U.S. Postal Service or law enforcement before they arrived.

title: Attorneys for Rep. Ilhan Omar accuse DOJ of violating judge's orders
summary: Omar's attorneys asked the government to immediately return the congresswoman's property, and also demanded all video and audio recordings of the search be preserved.
story: Attorneys for Representative Ilhan Omar have accused the Justice Department of violating a magistrate judge's order by failing to follow certain protocols designed to safeguard her constitutional interests as a member of Congress during the search of her home in Washington, D.C.

In the Oct. 16 letter, Omar's attorneys Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz asked the government to immediately return the congresswoman's property, and they also demanded all video and audio recordings of the search be preserved.

"This vindictive, retributive, and politically motivated criminal investigation into one of the President's chief congressional critics violates Representative Omar's constitutional rights and threatens the separation of powers," they wrote in the letter, which was reviewed by CBS News.
In a statement, a Justice Department spokesperson disputed the claims in the letter, saying it was "riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies."

"Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do," the spokesperson said. "Leaking a letter to the press right after sending it is not good faith. It is a publicity play."

Agents from the Homeland Security Investigations executed a search warrant at Omar's home on Monday, as part of a sprawling criminal investigation into her family's history for evidence of possible fraud and false statements in their immigration paperwork.

Her personal cellphone was among the materials seized in the search, CBS News previously reported, and grand jury subpoenas were also issued just days before the search to some of Omar's family members.
The search warrant was first presented to a magistrate judge in U.S. District Court about a week before it was executed.

Prosecutors and the judge engaged in a lengthy back-and-forth, after the judge raised concerns that the search warrant failed to incorporate any protocols to protect Omar's legislative privileges under the Constitution's speech and debate clause, CBS News previously reported.

Those protections stem from the 2007 United States v. Rayburn House Office Building D.C. Circuit Court case, which held that in a criminal investigation of a sitting member of Congress, the executive branch can't review information that is seized in a search without allowing that member to first screen it for legislative privilege.
Initially, prosecutors tried to argue the case shouldn't apply because the search was being carried out at Omar's home, and not at her congressional office, CBS News previously reported.
In the letter to the Justice Department, Omar's lawyers alleged several key requirements imposed by the judge had been violated.

HSI agents, for example, were supposed to notify both Omar and the House of Representatives Office of General Counsel of the execution of the search warrant — a step Omar's lawyers say never took place.

Agents also allegedly prevented her from contacting her attorney for more than an hour after the search started, the letter alleges, even though she and her counsel were supposed to be presented with a copy of the search warrant at the outset.
The timing of the search warrant and issuance of grand jury subpoenas in the case have raised eyebrows among many veteran former prosecutors.

Such overt investigative steps involving a sitting member of Congress so close to an election appear to run afoul of internal Justice Department guidelines, which state that prosecutors and agents should avoid taking overt investigative steps that could affect the outcome of an election or give one candidate an advantage or disadvantage.

Omar's lawyers also raised these same concerns in their letter to the department, saying: "Historically, the Department has refrained from this type of investigative activity so close to an election, so as to avoid even the appearance of politically motivated law enforcement actions. But the political motivations behind this pre-election investigation and search are clear as day. For the reasons given above, this search was neither justified nor lawful."

Omar has long been a frequent political target by President Trump and his allies. Mr. Trump has also made derogatory comments about her Somali heritage and her religion, and he has repeatedly accused her of immigration fraud.

"There is no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status," her attorneys wrote in the letter to DOJ, adding the search of her home "arose from a years-old, tired conspiracy theory concerning conduct stretching back decades."
Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin made unusually public remarks about the nonpublic criminal investigation in a podcast on Friday, calling it a "strong case."

In an interview with Andrew Kolvet, who hosts "The Charlie Kirk Show," Mullin volunteered that multiple warrants had been served on Monday, adding that a judge had authorized the enforcement action and investigators expected to present their case to a grand jury.

It is unusual for federal officials to speak openly about ongoing criminal investigations beyond confirming a court-authorized search was conducted, in part due to due process protections and grand jury secrecy rules.

title: Vance calls El-Sayed a "weasel" as Michigan Senate race heats up
summary: Abdul El-Sayed told Michigan voters the state's U.S. Senate race could go down "as one of the ugliest campaigns in modern history."
story: Marquette, Michigan –  After being called a "weasel" who should "shut his mouth" by Vice President JD Vance, Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed said he was something else instead.

"No, no, no. What you're talking about is a f****** Wolverine. You could take your Buckeye and go shove it somewhere else," El-Sayed, a Michigan alumnus, told a crowd of over 1,300 in the Upper Peninsula of the state. Vance was previously Ohio's senator and is an Ohio State University graduate.

Vance, President Trump and Republicans have sought to portray El-Sayed, an epidemiologist who has led city and county health departments in Michigan, as an Islamic extremist. Late Thursday night, Mr. Trump in a Truth Social video accused El-Sayed of being a "Muslim radical" and a "Muslim Brotherhood Member," though there is no evidence for either claim.

During his own rally in Monroe on Thursday, Vance criticized El-Sayed's past critical comments about America's history, and said "it's clear – Abdul doesn't love this community, Democrat or Republican."

"He wants to litigate ancient grievances with your tax dollars, and he wants to use the grievances of faraway lands to punish you. Well, I say, on November the third, send a message to Abdul El-Sayed: Punish him, don't send him to Washington D.C," Vance told the crowd.

Vance and El-Sayed have traded jabs before. After an El-Sayed post questioned whether Vance's grandfather would have accepted second lady Usha Vance, an Indian-American, Vance called him "very, very evil."
In response to Vance's latest comments, El-Sayed said the remarks were intended "to raise questions about my commitment to America."
"I got a front-row seat to what my life might have been had I not been born in America. So don't lecture me about America," El-Sayed countered, in reference to trips he has taken to Egypt.

"In America, we don't discriminate against people for who they love, how they identify, how they pray, the color of their skin. We believe in an America big enough for all of us. So don't you dare come from Ohio to lecture me about America. You don't know a damn thing about America," he added.
"One of the ugliest campaigns in modern history"
Holding the Michigan Senate seat is critical to Democrats' efforts to flip control of the U.S. Senate into their hands in November. But the race has turned especially contentious this month.

At a campaign stop in Iron Mountain on Thursday, El-Sayed said the race could go down "as one of the ugliest campaigns in modern history," a reference to Republican claims that El-Sayed has ties to foreign terrorist groups.

The claims in part stem from old social media posts made by his half-sister, first reported by the conservative outlet The Washington Free Beacon, when she wrote about their mother's activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during college in the 1970s.

In 2012, after a Muslim Brotherhood candidate won the presidential race in Egypt, she wrote that her family "has long been MB" but added that she has "always felt that it has navigated the political sphere poorly/destructively."

El-Sayed has denied any ties to the Islamist organization and has criticized the attacks as being tied to his Muslim faith. He said after his parents divorced, he was raised by his father and stepmother in Michigan and did not see his mother for years and did not talk with her about any activism in the 1970s.

"My mom and my sister are not running for office. I'm running for office. Judge me by my actions and my work, but please do not assume that because I might pray differently than anybody who's ever held this office, that somehow I am not deeply committed to this Constitution," he added.

Islamophobic rhetoric on the campaign trail, including claims that El-Sayed himself is a terrorist, has increased in recent weeks. Far-right instigator Jake Lang and others held signs that read "Abdul = Terrorist In A Suit" at the protest of an El-Sayed event last weekend. The Rogers campaign condemned Lang's appearance and said it has no affiliation with him.

Republican protesters also showed up outside the first two stops of El-Sayed's tour on Thursday. They held signs with messages criticizing his "Medicare for All" platform, declaring "The United States Will Always Be A Christian Nation" and urging voters to "Keep Terror Out Of Congress."
On the campaign trail with Rogers last weekend, Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana quipped that El-Sayed "sleeps in a Bin Laden jersey."
Asked by CBS News Thursday if he thinks El-Sayed is a terrorist, Rogers replied, "Look at the data. It's pretty clear."
But speaking to reporters in Detroit on Friday about the recent focus on El-Sayed's religion in the Senate race, Rogers said the race "has never been about how you pray."

"You get to pray any way you want, and I passionately believe that. It is about your ideology and how you think. We can't let this be a campaign deciding to hunker down because they say it's Islamophobic or racist, or fill-in-the-blank," he said, according to Fox 2 Detroit.
El-Sayed campaigns in GOP strongholds as Rogers targets Detroit
The Upper Peninsula of Michigan accounts for just 3% of the state's total population, and Republicans have easily won the area since 2016. Mr. Trump won all but one of the area's 15 counties in 2024.

El-Sayed took his campaign bus there anyway, and brought Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York with him as he tried to appeal to disaffected Republican and independent voters frustrated with the economy and the Iran War.

At packed stops, Ocasio-Cortez addressed the GOP attack ads and mailers targeting El-Sayed, and said they were trying to create a "caricature of him, so that you close your ears before you even hear what this man has to say."
Ocasio-Cortez transferred $1 million to El-Sayed's campaign. Asked about the contribution on Friday, she told reporters it's "the first time that I've made a transfer of this kind."
"I believe so deeply in how important this state is. I believe so deeply in the transformational power of Abdul's leadership," she said.
Asked by CBS News about the vice president's attacks on El-Sayed, Ocasio-Cortez said: "I think he's on the back foot right now."

"You've got gas anywhere between five to six a gallon, depending on where you are in the country, and they know that they need to be putting these distractions out around Abdul El-Sayed because the one person they don't want you hearing about is Mike Rogers," Ocasio-Cortez said. "So, JD Vance can say whatever he wants to say, but the reality is that this administration's record has been horrific for working-class Americans."
Independent voter John Haigh says he's backing El-Sayed, and said the higher grocery, gas and diesel prices are a reason more conservative-leaning voters in the area are considering El-Sayed.
"You should always be looking at the other side and hearing what they have to say, not just negative ads," Haigh told CBS News at the Iron Mountain event.

About an hour away, in the small town of Escanaba, Republican voter Al Hansen said he likes El-Sayed's ideas on affordability. But Hansen is still backing Rogers, in part because he's skeptical of the feasibility of a government-run healthcare plan and the barrage of TV ads have not convinced him.

"How are you gonna do it? Of course, in a 30-second commercial they don't have time to explain that. It's very hard," Hansen conceded when spoke with CBS News at a coffee shop nearby El-Sayed's event.
Republican groups have spent over $119.2 million on TV ads in Michigan, compared to $86.6 million for Democratic groups, according to advertisement tracking firm AdImpact.

Last weekend in Highland, Michigan, Rogers dismissed El-Sayed's attempts to whittle away at his GOP base of support. He then pointed to his own wooing of typically Democratic enclaves in the Detroit metro area – with heavily Jewish and Black populations whom El-Sayed's primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, won decisively.

"He really needs to shore up his base down here. That tells me they are desperate," Rogers told reporters. He claimed their internal polling shows they will get between 60% to 70% of Jewish Democratic voters who have been critical of El-Sayed's positions in opposition against the U.S.' relationship with Israel.

El-Sayed and his campaign have pointed to conversations he's had with the Jewish community, and support from Democratic statewide Jewish politicians, like Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel and Sen. Elissa Slotkin.

Rogers has also targeted the Black vote in Detroit through appearances at churches and closed door conversations. He argues his education and housing plans appeal to Detroit voters, and that he is finding a "whole new coalition that's coming to us."

"Some of those areas in Detroit feel pretty neglected. They haven't had people down and around paying attention to them," Rogers told CBS News at Vance's rally Thursday. He added, "We even went into a church the other day who said they hadn't had a Republican cross the threshold...in 76 years."

"He's showing up more than a Republican would," Detroit-area Reverend Charles Williams II said of Rogers, adding that he's tapping into existing tensions between some Black and Arab-American communities in the Detroit Metro area.

El-Sayed, who campaigned in Detroit on Wednesday with The Black Slate organization, could see a boost soon amongst Black voters with some high-profile visits. Former President Barack Obama is set to rally with him later this month, and Rep. Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts is campaigning for him this weekend.

At an event hosted by The Black Slate Wednesday, El-Sayed highlighted his work as a health official in Wayne County, which encompasses Detroit, and said his "story in America does not happen" without the organizing and history of the Civil Rights Movement.

He was asked about his commitment to the community and why voters should believe these appearances aren't "one off" conversations for the political season. El-Sayed responded that "it is not enough to get elected."

But Democratic Detroit councilwoman Mary Waters, who is undecided on who she'll vote for in the Senate race, also acknowledged the substantial GOP outreach to the Black community. She said while El-Sayed's campaign is also doing outreach, she thinks voters are disenchanted with what they see as ineffective Democratic governance.

"The majority of voters vote straight Democrat. But there is an outside chance…that the 30% who have not committed to anybody, Rogers could break in and get some of those votes," she said. "But it's a big state. And he still has to do outreach with his party as well."

title: Mars rover sets new driving record on surface of another world
summary: NASA's Perseverance Mars rover has set a new record for the longest distance traveled on the surface of another planet, the space agency said.
story: NASA's Perseverance rover set an otherworldly driving record this week, traveling the farthest of any vehicle ever on the surface of another planet.

The space agency said its rover, which has been exploring Mars since 2021, had driven 28.1 miles as of Sunday, exceeding the previous record set by NASA's Opportunity rover, which drove 28.06 miles during its 15-year exploration of the red planet, from 2004 to 2018.

Perseverance reached the milestone distance while traveling along the western rim of of Mars' Jezero Crater, where the rover has been tasked with investigating what scientists believe may be some of the oldest terrain in the solar system. They hope Perseverance will find traces of ancient hydrothermal systems — underground networks that heat water — in that area.

The rover has made important discoveries at the Jezero Crater since first landing on Mars in February 2021. Several years into its mission, Perseverance had collected enough data for scientists to develop a timeline of the crater's formation, dividing its history into "three major periods" after water originally entered it. In 2023, NASA said it was possible that microbial life once existed there.

Perseverance has been able to cover as much ground as it has in a relatively short time, compared with its predecessors, because of its self-driving capabilities. The rover is equipped with an autonomous navigation system, called AutoNav, that allows it to collect images of surrounding terrain, map out hazards and plan its own route as it's rolling along.

Scientists overseeing the rover have dubbed that skill "thinking while driving." They said Perseverance is also able to navigate itself while traveling at top speeds, up to 1,351 feet over the course of one sol, which is how scientists count a single solar day on Mars.

"It is an honor to be working on Perseverance at a moment when the technology has evolved to the point that drives like these are routine," said Steven Lee, the project manager of the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in a statement.

Lee said the rover has "blown well past" the 12.4 miles of driving initially expected during the mission, and now, it's likely that Perseverance will "keep adding to this record for many years to come."
NASA said it recently extended the Perseverance mission to allow to explore the rim of the Jezero Crater until the end of 2028.

title: Spectacular launch sends cargo ship on voyage to space station
summary: Along with crew supplies and equipment, the Cargo Dragon is delivering two rollout solar arrays to complete a major power system upgrade.
story: A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket boosted an unpiloted Dragon cargo ship into orbit Tuesday, setting up a rendezvous with the International Space Station early Thursday to deliver more than 6,300 pounds of research materials, spare parts and crew supplies.
Also on board are two new rollout solar array blankets, the final sets in a major upgrade to compensate for age-related degradation of the station's original eight solar wings.

Six "IROSA" blankets were installed during spacewalks starting in June 2021. The seventh and eighth IROSA arrays on board the Cargo Dragon will be installed during spacewalks later this month and in early November.

The Falcon booster's nine first-stage engines thundered to life at 6:33 a.m. EDT, throttled up and smoothly pushed the rocket away from Pad 40 at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station atop 1.7 million pounds of thrust.

Two-and-a-half minutes later, now out of the dense lower atmosphere, the first stage fell away and headed back toward Cape Canaveral for a return-to-launch-site landing while the second stage continued the climb to orbit.

At almost the same moment, viewers at the Kennedy Space Center were treated to a stunning view of the space station passing 260 miles overhead, a brilliant "star" moving from southwest to northeast. The Falcon 9's launch was timed to ensure the rocket climbed away into that same orbital plane, a requirement for rendezvous missions.

As the second stage continued the ascent, the exhaust plume from its single engine expanded in the low pressure of the extreme upper atmosphere, growing into an enormous teardrop shape visible for hundreds of miles around, backlit by the rising sun.

The first stage, meanwhile, heralded by two ground-shaking sonic booms, landed within a few hundred feet of its launch pad at 6:41 a.m. One minute and 10 seconds later, the second-stage engine shut down and the Cargo Dragon was released to fly on its own.
If all goes well, the spacecraft will catch up with the space station Thursday, moving in for an automated docking at the forward Harmony module's space-facing port at 11 a.m.

The Cargo Dragon is loaded with more than 6,300 pounds of supplies and equipment, including 844 pounds of supplies for the crew, 1,307 pounds of science gear, 417 pounds of spacewalk equipment and 880 pounds of vehicle hardware and computer gear.

Also on board: fresh food for the crew, including "oranges, apples, grapefruit, tomatoes, blueberries, baby carrots and mini sweet peppers," said Bill Spetch, space station program manager. "There's also the always popular pizza kit, cookies and candy, as well as some special holiday items."
The IROSA solar arrays, tipping the scales at 2,635 pounds on Earth, are mounted in the Dragon's unpressurized trunk section.
Each IROSA blanket generates 20 kilowatts of power and, acting in concert with the original arrays, boosts power output back to factory-fresh levels.

"The new arrays are installed on top, over in front of the existing solar arrays," Dana Weigel, director of low-Earth orbit operations at the Johnson Space Center, said earlier. "The exposed portion of the old arrays will still be generating power in parallel with the new arrays."

"Those new IROSA arrays have solar cells on them that are more efficient than our original cells, they have a higher energy density, and together in combination, they generate more power than what (an) original array, when it was new, did on its own," Weigel said.

title: Mars rover sets new driving record on surface of another world
summary: NASA's Perseverance Mars rover has set a new record for the longest distance traveled on the surface of another planet, the space agency said.
story: NASA's Perseverance rover set an otherworldly driving record this week, traveling the farthest of any vehicle ever on the surface of another planet.

The space agency said its rover, which has been exploring Mars since 2021, had driven 28.1 miles as of Sunday, exceeding the previous record set by NASA's Opportunity rover, which drove 28.06 miles during its 15-year exploration of the red planet, from 2004 to 2018.

Perseverance reached the milestone distance while traveling along the western rim of of Mars' Jezero Crater, where the rover has been tasked with investigating what scientists believe may be some of the oldest terrain in the solar system. They hope Perseverance will find traces of ancient hydrothermal systems — underground networks that heat water — in that area.

The rover has made important discoveries at the Jezero Crater since first landing on Mars in February 2021. Several years into its mission, Perseverance had collected enough data for scientists to develop a timeline of the crater's formation, dividing its history into "three major periods" after water originally entered it. In 2023, NASA said it was possible that microbial life once existed there.

Perseverance has been able to cover as much ground as it has in a relatively short time, compared with its predecessors, because of its self-driving capabilities. The rover is equipped with an autonomous navigation system, called AutoNav, that allows it to collect images of surrounding terrain, map out hazards and plan its own route as it's rolling along.

Scientists overseeing the rover have dubbed that skill "thinking while driving." They said Perseverance is also able to navigate itself while traveling at top speeds, up to 1,351 feet over the course of one sol, which is how scientists count a single solar day on Mars.

"It is an honor to be working on Perseverance at a moment when the technology has evolved to the point that drives like these are routine," said Steven Lee, the project manager of the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in a statement.

Lee said the rover has "blown well past" the 12.4 miles of driving initially expected during the mission, and now, it's likely that Perseverance will "keep adding to this record for many years to come."
NASA said it recently extended the Perseverance mission to allow to explore the rim of the Jezero Crater until the end of 2028.

title: With Tesla Roadster debut, Elon Musk shows "flying cars are real"
summary: Elon Musk unveiled Tesla's new Roadster, which uses high-pressure air thrusters to leave the road entirely during a livestreamed event at his SpaceX facility in Texas.
story: Tesla CEO Elon Musk unveiled what he described as a "flying" car, equipped with thrusters, during a livestreamed event at his SpaceX rocket company's facility on Thursday.
Technical and regulatory challenges have so far prevented the much-hyped flying car sector from getting off the ground.
Musk revealed Tesla's new Roadster sports car during a launch event at a SpaceX test facility in Texas.

During the demo, which was livestreamed on Tesla's X account, the car launched from a ramp that curled over so the vehicle was upside down, appearing to defy gravity by clinging to the surface before flying off the end, and then rolled over 180 degrees midair to land on its wheels.
"Flying cars are real," Musk said during the event, adding that the vehicle's "success is not guaranteed" but "it will probably work."
Musk said the car was equipped with "ultra high-pressure air tanks" to propel itself into the air.
The tech billionaire described the development as "what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company," referring to Tesla and SpaceX.
The vehicle would go into production in 2028, he said. Prices were not announced.
Tesla's website notes that the planned flying model is not approved for public road use.

Would-be buyers can place a reservation online, with a $5,000 deposit, for a non-flying model of the Roadster. A limited-edition Thrust model is also promised online but cannot be reserved. Tesla's website says the Rocket model, with its "full flight system," will be offered by invitation only.

"The Roadster will not move the volume or revenue needle, with production likely limited, and investors should not model it as a growth driver," Wall Street analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said in a research note. "What it does is restore the brand halo at the top of the market and put a spotlight on the engineering stack a week before the FY3Q26 print on October 21st."

It wasn't immediately clear what government agency would have oversight of the vehicle, CBS News senior transportation and national correspondent Kris Van Cleave reports. A senior U.S. Transportation Department official expressed some skepticism to CBS News that the vehicle will actually be able to take off, but acknowledged there wasn't a clear answer.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration typically has regulatory oversight of vehicles but delegates safety certification to the automaker. NHTSA didn't immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.
The Federal Aviation Administration told CBS News the vehicle doesn't meet the agency's definition of an aircraft.

The concept of flying cars has been around almost as long as motor vehicles themselves, with American aviation pioneer Glenn Curtiss debuting the first flying car prototype in 1917. But successful designs have been pursued more seriously only in recent years as electric motors and high-performance batteries have advanced.

Ives said the Roadster shows how Tesla and SpaceX can collaborate. The new vehicle "puts the Tesla and SpaceX relationship on the table in a tangible way, with propulsion, pressure-vessel, and control hardware developed at the rocket company sitting on a Tesla product, which in our view strengthens the case for the two companies operating as one engineering platform over time," he said.

Musk — a major GOP political donor known for an often close but sometimes tumultuous relationship with President Trump — has thrust his companies to the forefront of several major industries, and he continues pushing into new ones.

SpaceX announced a week ago that it had agreed to buy licenses for radio airwaves that will enable its Starlink Mobile satellite business to provide cellular service inside buildings, a move the company said would allow it to "become a major mobile carrier in the U.S."
"This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America," Musk said in an Oct. 8 social media post.

title: Tech stocks tumble as AI debt fears rattle Wall Street
summary: Wall Street is pulling back from chipmakers and other tech companies amid concerns about the debt incurred to build out AI.
story: Financial markets slumped on Friday as investors bailed on technology stocks amid concerns that companies exposed to artificial intelligence are starting to wobble.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite tumbled 573 points, or 2.1%, to end at 26,140, closing out its worst week since June. The broader S&P 500 and blue-chip Dow Industrial Average sank 1.1% and 0.3%, respectively.

Chipmakers and other tech companies have been under pressure this week as investors worry about the heavy borrowing associated with the emergence of AI and the rapid buildout of thousands of data centers required to provide computing power for AI models.

So-called neocloud companies like CoreWeave, which provide the brute computing power AI models need to function, were particularly hard hit. That's because they are financing much of their capital expenditures through debt and equity issuance rather than cash flow, raising investor concerns about mounting debt, market analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, told CBS News.

Shares of CoreWeave slid nearly 12% on Friday and dropped roughly 24% this week as investors nervously eye its mounting debt. Micron Technology fell 5.6%, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 6%, Broadcom was down 4.5% and Intel lost 5.8%.
Elsewhere on Wall Street, Tesla shares fell 2.1% after the electric vehicle company unveiled a new Roadster sports car that appears capable of thrusting itself into the air.

The downturn on Friday came amid concern about whether the AI company Anthropic, soon set to go public, will be able to maintain its revenue momentum, Crisafulli said in a note to investors. Anthropic investors are now considering valuing the company at $1.5 trillion, down from the original target of $2 trillion, Reuters reported on Thursday.
Inflation moving in wrong direction
Also rattling investors this week were fresh signs that U.S. inflation is increasing and moving further away from the Federal Reserve's 2% annual target.

Yields on the 10-year U.S. Treasury bonds — a key benchmark for mortgages, credit cards and other loans — held steady at 5.1% on Friday. Earlier this month, bond yields surged to their highest level in more than two decades amid concerns over inflation and rising U.S. government debt.

The hot inflation readings this week could spur the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its next meeting on Oct. 28-29, according to some economists. For now, most Wall Street traders expect the central bank to keep its short-term rate unchanged, but the odds of a rate hike at the Fed's December meeting have jumped to 74.3% from 50.2% a month ago, according to CME FedWatch, which tracks Fed funds futures prices.

On Friday, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh offered no hints about potential interest rate policy moves while attending a meeting of financial leaders in Bangkok. The Fed hiked rates at its last meeting in September, bringing the federal funds rate to between 3.75% and 4% — its highest level since December 2025.

title: iPhone Duo already backordered until 2027 as pre-order sales soar
summary: Consumer demand for Apple's first foldable phone is strong despite the device's hefty $1,999 price tag.
story: Apple is seeing strong demand for its new foldable iPhone, with supplies quickly selling out after pre-order sales opened on Friday.

"Apple opened iPhone Duo pre-orders this morning, and the early read looks robust in our view, with demand for Cupertino's first foldable running well ahead of supply out of the gates," Wall Street analyst Dan Ives, a partner at Yorkville Ives, said in a research note.

The pre-order window for the Duo opened on Friday at 8 a.m. ET on apple.com and in the Apple Store app. Within minutes, the estimated delivery of the phone was pushed back past Oct. 23, the device's official launch date, and into next year. As of Friday afternoon, the Apple phone was backordered until late January.
"It's been 3 minutes, and it's sold out at every store around the NYC/CT area," Max Weinbach, an analyst for the market research firm Creativestrat, said on X.
Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how many pre-order requests it received.

Apple's new CEO, John Ternus, announced the iPhone Duo last month. The Duo lets users split the screen to use two different apps on the device, or two windows of the same website for uses such as comparison shopping.

Prices start at $1,999 for a device with 256 GB of storage. When folded, it's about the size of a passport. The full display is the largest of any Apple phone, resembling more of an iPad than an iPhone.
Ternus also announced the iPhone 18 at Apple's annual fall showcase, which went on sale last month.

Ives thinks demand for the Duo will remain strong into 2027, with many iPhone users planning to upgrade. He projects Apple will sell around 10 million Duos in the next few quarters and up to 25 million in 2027.

title: Amazon launches new AI devices that can listen and take notes
summary: The products include a silicone wristband that can be clipped to clothing and a device that magnetically attaches to the back of a phone.
story: Amazon launched two new AI gadgets on Thursday that the company says can listen to conversations, compose notes and issue reminders.

The first, the Bee Frontier, is a silicone wristband that can also be clipped to clothing and retails for $74.99. Amazon also announced the Bee Eclipse, a credit card-sized device that magnetically attaches to the back of a phone and goes for $99.99.
The new tech offerings are engineered by Bee, an AI wearable maker that Amazon acquired last year.

Equipped with microphones, Bee's "personal AI" devices transcribe meetings or everyday conversations, helping people document moments hands-free. The devices can then recommend "personalized goals and actions" based on the conversation, Amazon said.
"It takes note of the details you might otherwise forget and turns them into useful conversation summaries, to-dos, reminders, and insights," the company said in its release.
If someone is on a phone call planning a vacation, for example, the Bee Frontier or Bee Eclipse will create a summary of the trip, documenting details such as flight times or hotel reservations.

Amazon said users can also connect Bee to existing apps such as Gmail, Google Calendar, and Microsoft Outlook, allowing the AI technology to draft follow-up emails or create calendar invites based on what was discussed. The Bee devices can also be linked to Amazon's Alexa+ and Amazon.com.

Users can get conversation summaries, recaps and 14 days of memory for free; if they want more advanced capabilities, such as integration with Alexa+ and Amazon.com and suggested to-dos, they'll need a Bee Pro subscription, which costs $11.99 per month.

Amazon emphasized Bee's privacy protections, noting that "no one, including Amazon, can access your data." The audio recordings are deleted after the Bee devices transcribe them, and no one can access your data unless you share it, the company said.

The Bee devices are part of a trillion-dollar market of AI gadgets that companies are marketing to consumers. Meta recently announced Muse, an AI assistant that comes in the form of a pocket-sized keychain. Microsoft, OpenAI and Samsung are among the other companies that have introduced AI-powered products aimed at consumers.

title: FTC issues subpoenas to Anthropic and OpenAI over safety incidents
summary: The demands come amid mounting public concerns about the potential risks posed by frontier AI models.
story: The Federal Trade Commission has subpoenaed Anthropic and OpenAI to gather information about potential consumer protection violations, a spokesperson for the agency confirmed.

The development, first reported by Axios, comes just two weeks after the FTC said it was investigating the artificial intelligence companies as part of a probe it launched this summer. The agency declined further comment about the probe.

The FTC is seeking documents on safety incidents, privacy policies and safeguards at Anthropic and OpenAI, Axios reported. The companies have come under public scrutiny in recent months after several incidents in which their AI models went rogue and hacked into websites.

The agency, which sent civil investigative demands to Anthropic and OpenAI on Wednesday, will also issue subpoenas to third-party organizations at a later date, according to Axios, which cited a person familiar with the matter.

The FTC could compel Anthropic and OpenAI to testify before Congress about their products, a move that would allow the government to press the companies about the safety of their technology as the public grows increasingly wary about its potential harms.

A recent poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that 64% of U.S. adults think AI is developing "too fast." Eight in 10 said it's "extremely" or "very" important for the U.S. government to ensure that AI stays under human control.

President Trump has resisted calls to slow the development of AI, saying that the technology is vital to U.S. national interests. He recently announced the creation of a "Super Intelligence Force" to coordinate with the federal government on AI matters and engage with consumers, public interest groups and other stakeholders.

title: On dating apps, men use AI to put their best face forward
summary: How much AI is too much when it comes to finding love on the apps? "It's very subtle," one dating app user said of his AI-enhanced photos.
story: Marissa, a 31-year-old Boston resident, downloaded dating apps because she is looking for love. But more and more, she finds herself looking for something else: AI-free photos.

The marketing professional said she routinely comes across dating app profiles that appear to be digitally altered. Usually, the changes are minor and can be easily made using tools like Photoshop, such as editing someone out of a photo. Sometimes, however, the photo appears to be completely AI-generated, she told CBS News, citing a photo she came across on Bumble of a man dressed in a suit tiling a bathroom wall.
"AI aside, I'm not sure what the appeal is there," she said (Marissa asked to withhold her surname for privacy reasons).

Numerous women on TikTok also report spotting photos of men on dating apps that appear to be AI-generated. Their accounts demonstrate how AI is blurring the line between what's real and what's fake in the already fraught arena of online dating. They also raise ethical questions about how far is too far when it comes to manipulating your online persona.

"People want authentic connections and conversations," Kathryn Coduto, an assistant professor at Boston University who studies dating apps, told CBS News in an email. "I think AI has made people more wary and skeptical of others, especially people they don't know."

Of course, dating app users have long relied on filters and other editing tools to polish their photos. But AI tools are upping the ante, allowing people to create high-quality images within seconds, and in some cases, fabricate fake scenes.

"A dater has to think about how they're going to capture someone's attention in a few seconds or less," Coduto told CBS News. "This might mean making your photo look a little better than it might have before."
To be sure, this practice isn't exclusive to men. However, they appear more likely to use AI to spruce up their dating profiles than women, Coduto added.
"So far, men are more interested in AI in the dating space, which isn't surprising," Coduto said. "Women tend to receive more matches and messages, so men have a harder time standing out."
The "digital stylist" who helps men AI their photos

AI can create obvious distortions when it generates photos, such as omitting a finger from someone's hand. For Marissa, a telltale sign is the person's face, which sometimes looks "waxy" in AI-generated photos, she said.
Still, as technology improves, it's becoming harder to distinguish a real photo from one created by AI models.

Lana Li, a Brooklyn, New York, dating consultant who runs the Substack "Love Me Like a Robot," calls herself a "digital stylist." She uses AI to help men level up their dating app photos, and defends using the technology as long as the photos still genuinely represent who they are.

"I can take a picture of somebody and then put them in a different outfit or change their hairstyle a little bit, or put different shoes on them," she told CBS News. "Or if I think their body language doesn't look confident in the picture, I will have [ChatGPT] change that."
The 37-year-old also uses FaceApp to change men's facial expressions. She said the edits are subtle, such as slightly lifting the corner of someone's mouth to make them look "friendlier."

Despite her liberal approach to using AI, there are lines Li is unwilling to cross. For example, one client asked her to digitally alter a photo so that his head was on a marathon runner's body — a request she declined.
"I told him, 'I can't work with you if you want to not represent yourself accurately,'" she said.

Two men who spoke to CBS News on the condition of anonymity to maintain their privacy told CBS News they've used AI in their online dating photos, but in ways they feel stop short of being misleading and remain true to who they are.
A ban on Hinge
One man, a 30-year-old tech employee and client of Li's, said she used ChatGPT to digitally clothe him in more professional garb and to tame his frizzy hair.

"It's very subtle," the New York City resident said, saying he still looked like himself, even with the edits. He emphasized that he doesn't want to "catfish" anyone — a concern for singles even in the absence of AI.

Another man is pulling back after one of his AI photos backfired. The 50-something-year-old New York City resident said he fed photos of himself into Aragon.ai, an AI headshot generator, which produced a picture of him standing on a Manhattan roof with a sunset in the background. It immediately drew hits on his Hinge profile.

"This picture generally got the most likes," he told CBS News. "Now that could just be because it was the first thing they saw. But regardless, it was proving to be effective, and women seemed to like it."
That was, until Hinge banned him. He managed to get his account back but ultimately decided to delete the sunset photo, suspecting it was the reason for his removal from the app.
"How much AI am I OK with?"

Most popular dating apps have policies that limit the use of AI-generated images in people's profiles. Hinge emphasizes the importance of authenticity on its website, noting that people should be able to discern "fact from fiction."
"If you decide to include generative AI images, audio, or video in your profile, it should not be used to misrepresent yourself or your intentions," the company says on its AI policy page.

Hinge also uses automated tools and human reviewers to detect and remove "prohibited material," according to the company's terms of service. If users see suspicious AI material, they can confidentially report it through the app or online.

A spokesperson for Match Group, which owns Hinge, Tinder and a handful of other dating apps, told CBS that as generative AI evolves, the company is "watching closely and listening to daters, who tell us they want more transparency, more authenticity, and more confidence that a real person is on the other end."

Bumble also uses tools to detect and weed out AI-generated content, and lets users report profiles that feature such images. A spokesperson said the company prohibits inauthentic profiles, and Bumble's community guidelines bar the use of "artificially generated photos or enhanced photos to deceive others."

"We enforce this through a combination of AI-powered tools, human moderation, verification features and member reporting, and we take action based on the severity of a violation, up to and including permanently banning accounts," the spokesperson said.
Marissa, the 31-year-old who lives in Boston, said that when she sees a person's profile whose photos bear the hallmarks of AI, she chooses to move along.
"The dating pool is already challenging, and this is just another thing we have to grapple with," she said. "How much AI am I OK with?"

title: OpenAI employee accused of planting recording device in office
summary: A Saudi national who worked at OpenAI as an engineer is suspected of planting a recording device in one of the company's conference rooms.
story: An OpenAI employee suspected of secretly planting a recording device in one of the company's conference rooms has been arrested on criminal charges, the Justice Department said Tuesday.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested Friday and made his initial appearance in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California on Tuesday. Alfozan was charged with trying to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.
Prosecutors said that Alfozan had worked at OpenAI as an engineer since July 2025.

On Sept. 30, the company's employees discovered the audio recording device inserted into a USB port on the back of a television inside an executive conference room. The company later determined that the recording device had been concealed in toilet paper and installed about two days before it was discovered.

The meeting room where it was hidden was often used by OpenAI's employees to discuss highly confidential and proprietary matters, including research, product plans and business development, the Justice Department said.
In a statement, OpenAI said that after discovering the device, it contacted the FBI and has terminated the employee accused of planting it.

"The FBI's investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work. At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the company said.

"We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance. Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats."
FBI Director Kash Patel said in a post on X that the FBI and its partners had carried out the arrest and that the investigation is ongoing.

Alfozan's attorney, William Pernik, noted to CBS News that his client is presumed innocent, and cautioned against "jumping to conclusions at this very early stage of the case when very little information is known," or seeking to "politicize" a prosecution based on factors like nationality.

The criminal complaint, made public on Tuesday, alleged that Alfozan used a productivity tool to make inquiries about OpenAI's building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, and locations of "leadership and exec" and external partner meetings.

Other evidence gathered in the investigation, meanwhile, showed that a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse had also submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30, related to building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating and remote accessing a continuous audio recording device.
A photograph included in the complaint also shows that Alfozan entered the conference room where the device was hidden on Oct. 5 and looked behind the television.

That same day, the complaint says Alfozan left his bag unattended in another room, and the company's security personnel opened it and found his ID, wallet and another recording device similar to the one planted in the conference room.
Alfozan is due to appear in federal court again on Oct. 19 for a detention hearing.

title: Character.ai declares bankruptcy, citing legal and business woes
summary: AI company has faced multiple lawsuits from families who claimed their teenage children died by suicide or harmed themselves after using its platform.
story: Character.ai said it has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, with its chief executive attributing the chatbot provider's financial problems to "significant legal, regulatory and operational headwinds."

The company said it will continue operating as it seeks to sell its business, and added that The Walt Disney Co. has agreed to pay $20 million for a non-exclusive, perpetual license to Character.ai's intellectual property.

Character.ai's financial struggles follow scrutiny and litigation over its technology, which uses artificial intelligence to create custom bots consumers can chat with. In early 2026, Character.ai and Google, which had a licensing deal with the AI company, agreed to settle several lawsuits filed by families who claimed their teenage children died by suicide or harmed themselves after using Character.ai's platform.

The company settled a wrongful death lawsuit earlier in 2026 — the first filed in the U.S. against an AI company — with a Florida family who said their teen son died after conducting an emotional and sexual relationship with a chatbot known as "Dany." The family said in their lawsuit that Character.ai had no mechanisms in place to protect their son or notify an adult when teens were spending too much time interacting with Chatbots.
The company added several safety features designed with teens in mind after several lawsuits alleged its chatbots inappropriately interacted with underage users.

Several states have also sued Character.ai over its technology, with Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman alleging in January that its chatbots "preyed on children and led them into self-harm." In May, Pennsylvania sued Character.ai after one of its chatbots allegedly claimed to be a licensed psychiatrist in the state and provided a "fake Pennsylvania license number."
In a statement issued late Monday, Character.ai said it believes the company will be sold by late November or early December.

"After a comprehensive review of the available alternatives, the board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides the company with the best opportunity to maximize value for all stakeholders," Character.ai CEO Colin Adams said in the statement. "As we navigate this process, maintaining a safe and engaging user experience for our Character.ai community remains a top priority."
Is Character.ai shutting down?
The company said on Monday that its services continue to operate and that subscriptions remain active.
"If the service changes in a way that affects paid features, we intend to notify subscribers in advance," Character.ai said.

In a blog post, the company said customer data "continues to be protected under our Privacy Policy." That policy states that data Character.ai collects from users — including chat transcripts, voice recordings, and images and videos — could be disclosed in connection with a sale or a negotiation to sell the company or its assets.
"As a reminder, you can delete your account or export your data through the app or the Character.ai website," the company said.

title: Anthropic warns "AI worms" could soon infect smart home devices
summary: Small AI models could clone themselves and infect internet-connected devices such as smart TVs and appliances, the researchers warned.
story: Anthropic is sounding the alarm about a new risk posed by artificial intelligence: Self-replicating "AI worms" could soon infest your "smart" home devices.

In a report released on Monday, Anthropic safety researchers said small AI models may be only "months away" from gaining the ability to clone themselves and spread across internet-connected devices, such as smart ovens, TVs and vacuum cleaners. The ability to reproduce themselves without human control would make it hard to control such agents because there's "no centralized point to shut off," said Anthropic, which developed the Claude chatbot.
Stronger AI models are already capable of what the researchers called "end-to-end replication," a threshold they say smaller models could reach by year-end, according to Anthropic.
AI worms, a type of AI-powered malware, can quickly spread across networks and devices while evading detection, according to cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks.

Smart devices in people's homes, as well as internet-connected devices such as security cameras, are vulnerable given that internet-enabled devices tend to have weaker security protections, the Anthropic researchers said. In what they described as a worst-case scenario, a swarm of AI agents — bots that work together to accomplish a shared goal — could propagate across computer hardware using "replication schemes."

The researchers said they are unsure of what form these attacks could take, noting that the AI models could be distributed as "digital slime mold" or as more powerful models capable of hacking into data centers.

"We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay," the Anthropic researchers wrote in the report.

title: Air Force member dies in rappelling incident at UT San Antonio football game
summary: A service member was injured and later died after falling while rappelling from the ceiling of the University of Texas at San Antonio football stadium on Saturday.
story: A member of the U.S. Air Force was injured and later died after he fell while rappelling from the ceiling of the Alamodome stadium in San Antonio, Texas, on Saturday, ahead of a University of Texas at San Antonio football game.

The incident took place during a pregame ceremony, before the official kickoff of UTSA's annual Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans game against Navy, CBS affiliate KENS reported. The service member landed near the middle of the field after falling, a KENS photographer said.

Nellis Air Force Base Public Affairs issued a statement saying that the service member — identified as Tech. Sgt. Ian Patterson, a Tactical Air Control Party instructor assigned to the 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2, Joint Base San Antonio, Texas — was injured at the stadium and died at a local hospital. CBS News has reached out to Nellis AFB for additional comment.
Originally from Fort Stewart, Georgia, Patterson had served in the Air Force for 15 years, the base said Sunday night.

"This tragedy is felt deeply across the 57th Wing," Brig. Gen. Scott C. Mills, 57th Wing commander, said in a statement Sunday night. "Tech. Sgt. Patterson and his service mattered immensely to our wing, and to the family, friends, and teammates who had the privilege of knowing and serving alongside him. Our team is now focused on standing beside Ian's family, loved ones, and fellow Airmen as we navigate this profound loss together."

Patterson was one of four military service members who were scheduled to participate in a rappelling demonstration before Saturday's game. According to an Air Force website, they were part of a team of specialists who embed with Army and Marine units and help to direct air and artillery strikes from forward ground locations.
Part of their training includes learning to rapidly drop by rope, sometimes from helicopters that are 100 feet or more above the ground.

A video of the fall that was posted on social media showed Patterson, in combat fatigues, quickly descending to the ground feet first. The fall occurred with fans in the stands and a band assembled nearby on the field. He was treated on the field for several minutes and taken away on a gurney.
The incident is under investigation.

The game between the UTSA Roadrunners and the Navy Midshipmen still took place on Saturday. The American Conference said in a statement Sunday night that the decision to play the game was made before the airman's death had been confirmed.

"In accordance with conference bylaws and with the support of both participating member institutions, the conference made the decision to continue the game," the statement read in part. "Respect for the family's privacy and adherence to the military's notification process guided the decision to mitigate speculation about the service member's medical status and avoid additional distress for his family."

The conference also noted it was "heartbroken" about the death and said, "We extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends, teammates and members of the 57th Wing who had the privilege of serving with him. We honor his service and join the military community in mourning his loss."
After the game, the university issued a statement saying it was "deeply saddened by the incident that occurred at the start of tonight's football game."

"Our heartfelt thoughts and prayers are with the soldier who was affected, his family and his military colleagues," the statement said. "We recognize that members of our campus community may be emotionally affected by this incident and are activating wellbeing services to support our faculty, staff and students."
Taylor Eighmy, the university's president, also spoke out in the wake of the accident.

"What was intended to be a day of camaraderie, tradition and celebration has been marked by profound sadness," Eighmy said. "I want to extend my deepest and most heartfelt sympathies to the service member's family, his fellow airmen, squadron and all those whose lives have been touched by this heartbreaking tragedy."

In a separate statement, Lisa Campos, the vice president for intercollegiate athletics at UT San Antonio, added: "Moments like these remind us that we are all part of something much greater than a game."
After the game, which UTSA won 38-34, UTSA coach Jeff Traylor told reporters that the accident was "heartbreaking" and "tragic."

He said the team could see the effect that it had on the crowd of over 23,000 people as soon as players arrived on the field for the game, although Traylor had only been told there had been an "incident" that would delay the start of the game by about 10 minutes.
"You could tell the energy was just gone," he said. "It just really puts things in perspective. It really does."

title: Cindy Crawford and family break silence on Presley Gerber's death
summary: Cindy Crawford, Rande Gerber and their daughter, Kaia, have broken their silence for the first time since Presley Gerber's death​ last month.
story: Cindy Crawford, Rande Gerber and their daughter, Kaia, have broken their silence for the first time since Presley Gerber's death last month.

"We are beyond heartbroken to lose our beloved son and brother. We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years. He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever," a statement from the family shared on social media said. "We are so proud of how he showed up in the world, with kindness and vulnerability. We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain. Til we meet again our sweet boy. We love you forever, Mom, Dad and Kaia."

Presley Gerber died on Sept. 20 at a Santa Monica rehab facility at the age of 27. His cause of death remains deferred, according to the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner's website. But Santa Monica police have said his death was a suspected overdose. He was often open about his battles with addiction and mental health on his social media channels.

None of Presley Gerber's family members had publicly spoken about his death until Sunday. His parents, supermodel Cindy Crawford and businessman Rande Gerber, shared the same message on their Instagram accounts, while his younger sister, actor and model Kaia Gerber, shared her own.
"I love you the bluest, to the moon and back and back again, forever big brother," the caption said.
Her post also paid tribute to Presley Gerber, recounting experiences from their childhood and how she has struggled with a feeling of emptiness since his death.

"To say loving you was the easiest thing in the world would imply that it required any effort at all. I was born loving you. I will die loving you. There was never anything else," Kaia's message said. "I am learning how to love you when I canot see you. How to tell you something without picking up my phone to call you. How to be your sister in a world that I can't reach for you in."

title: Expedition to find Amelia Earhart's missing plane comes up empty
summary: The researchers said what they had hoped was the plane was "likely a collection of large trees" that had washed away, leaving a "single Y-shaped segment."
story: A mysterious object discovered near a remote Pacific island is not the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's missing plane, researchers said after an expedition to the site, dealing another setback to efforts to solve one of aviation's greatest mysteries nearly 90 years after the pilot disappeared.

"Evidence gathered at the Taraia Peninsula on Nikumaroro confirmed that the visual anomaly first seen in satellite imagery in 2020 was likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula's sandspit," the researchers said. "By the time the team arrived at the site, a good portion of the debris had fragmented and washed away, leaving only a single Y-shaped segment," which they said is what they had initially hoped was the plane.

The researchers said the reflective surface of the anomaly, which had led them to believe it could be metal, was the result of a carbonate veneer, noting other items found nearby were "similarly coated with a shiny concretized amalgam of coral sand."

On Oct. 14, a 17-member expedition team led by Purdue University's Steve Schultz and the Archaeological Legacy Institute's Richard Pettigrew launched an expedition to investigate a mysterious object that in aerial photos appeared to resemble possible wreckage of Earhart's Lockheed Electra 10-E plane.

Severe weather kept the research team aboard their ship for three of the five days allotted for the search, while limited fuel and supplies prevented them from extending the expedition. The search area was so remote, it took the team five days at sea to reach it.

The expedition focused on a lagoon off Nikumaroro, where researchers examined the Taraia Object, an anomaly spotted by a Navy veteran in satellite imagery during the COVID pandemic. Although visible in aerial photos dating back to 1938, the object went unnoticed until 2020. Pettigrew said before reaching it that they believed it could be metal rather than a tree, but further investigation was needed to confirm its identity.

"Amelia Earhart's spirit of courage and curiosity drove every step of the search," Pettigrew said Sunday. "We accomplished our goal to determine what the Taraia Object was, and we're deeply grateful to the private donors who shared our vision and made this journey possible. Our team remains in great spirits and proud of what was accomplished."

The team had developed plans to photograph and film the lagoon and Taraia Object before using magnetometers and sonar equipment to survey the area. Researchers then planned to retrieve the object for identification. The Archaeology Channel documented the expedition through short video updates on its Heritage Broadcasting Service streaming platform.
The research team previously said in a news release that there was "very strong" evidence that the object is Earhart's lost plane.

Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, disappeared on July 2, 1937, roughly 22,000 miles into their trip. Earhart was attempting to become the first female pilot to circle the world, and the first pilot to do so around the equator, Earth's widest point.
Recently, President Trump ordered the declassification of records related to Earhart.

Nikumaroro is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, located roughly halfway between Australia and Hawaii. The island lies about 400 miles southeast of Howland Island, where Earhart and Noonan were headed when they disappeared during their attempted flight around the world.

Pettigrew believes Earhart and Noonan landed on Nikumaroro and survived there for some time. He points to relics dating to the 1930s and to human remains discovered on the island, which were later lost as possible evidence. However, several competing theories about the aviator's disappearance have emerged over the decades, many of which lack conclusive evidence.

Researchers have spent decades searching for Earhart's plane, hoping its discovery could shed light on her disappearance. In 2024, an expedition team captured a sonar image of what appeared to be an aircraft on the ocean floor, but the object was later identified as a rock formation.
