title: Boy among 2 killed after truck drives onto Wichita soccer field
summary: A 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man were killed during a soccer game at Stryker Soccer Complex in Wichita, Kansas, according to police.
story: Two people were killed, and 11 were injured after a truck drove onto a soccer field Saturday in Wichita, Kansas, authorities said.

A 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man were killed during a soccer game at Stryker Soccer Complex, said Aaron Moses, a captain and executive officer with the Wichita Police Department. The boy was identified Sunday as Cole Adrian and the man as Nicholas Schafer, both of whom are from McPherson, Kansas, but they were not related, according to police.
Eleven people were transported to local hospitals with injuries that were not life-threatening, ranging in age from 5 years old to 68 years old, Moses said at a news conference.

The driver, a 34-year-old woman, was taken into custody and had been cooperative with the investigation, Moses said. Two juveniles were also inside the vehicle at the time, Moses said. It's unclear if the incident was intentional.

An investigation into the incident was ongoing, police said. No charges have been filed, and the driver was later released pending the results of toxicology testing and a mechanical examination of the vehicle, police said Sunday.
The city of Wichita said in a statement that all events at the soccer complex have been canceled until further notice.

"Today is a heartbreaking day for Wichita," Mayor Lily Wu said during a news conference on Saturday. "Families came to Stryker Soccer Complex to enjoy a Saturday afternoon watching their children play soccer. No one could have imagined the tragedy that would unfold."
In a statement on social media Sunday, U.S. Soccer said it was "heartbroken" by the tragedy and offered its condolences to the families impacted.

"The entire U.S. Soccer family stands with the soccer communities in Wichita and across Kansas during this incredibly difficult time," the statement said. "We will work closely with Wichita Youth Soccer to understand how we can best support the community in the days and weeks ahead."

title: Cows roam Kansas City highway after trailer plunged off overpass
summary: Dozens of cows fled the crash scene, resulting in other crashes and more calls to the police from the public, Kansas City police said.
story: Dozens of cattle spilled onto a street in Kansas City, Missouri, when a semitractor-trailer plunged off a highway overpass in the city's downtown area and onto a car early Sunday, shutting down some roads and setting off a search for the traumatized animals that survived.
The accident occurred shortly before 3 a.m. and the roundup of surviving cattle continued into the early afternoon, authorities said.
The driver of the truck and the driver of a vehicle the truck landed on sustained minor injuries and were treated at local hospitals, they said.

Kansas City Police Sgt. Phil DiMartino said that between 45 and 60 of the 120 to 130 cattle carried by the truck were killed when the tractor-trailer overturned and fell from the westbound I-70 curve over SB I-35.
Dozens of other cows fled the crash scene, resulting in other crashes and more calls to the police from the public, he said.
"It is believed all cows have now been accounted for," DiMartino said in an updated press release Sunday afternoon.

The accident occurred on a day when the Kansas City Chiefs were hosting the Los Angeles Chargers in a National Football League game. Major disruptions in game traffic were not anticipated by authorities because of the wide publicity that the accident had received.
Some of the cattle had walked several miles before they were captured, said Kansas City Fire Battalion Chief Michael Hopkins.
"It was a pretty nasty accident," Hopkins said.

Immediately after the accident, city authorities launched drones to track the cattle before a private company working together with the trucking company arrived with workers on horseback to round up the cattle, he said.
"More difficult has been getting the animals who did not survive," he added.

title: Falcons' Kendal Daniels leaves Bears game on stretcher after tackle
summary: On the way off the field, Kendal Daniels made a fist with his left hand.
story: Atlanta Falcons rookie linebacker Kendal Daniels was injured and left the field on a stretcher in the third quarter of Sunday's game against the Chicago Bears.

Daniels made a tackle on Bears tight end Colston Loveland and remained on the ground. He was attended to for several minutes and strapped to a board by trainers and left the field on a cart. His legs, body, head and shoulders were strapped down. On the way off the field, he made a fist with his left hand.
"Kendal Daniels is alert and has movement in all his extremities. He was taken to Grady Memorial Hospital for further evaluation," the Falcons said in a statement on social media.

Several defensive players on the Falcons were on one knee while Daniels was being attended to. Eventually, the entire Falcons bench came over on the field to support him. Multiple Bears players were also on one knee while Daniels was worked on. He was ruled out with a neck injury.
Daniels is a fourth-round draft pick out of Oklahoma. He has started six games and entered Sunday with 22 tackles this season.

title: CBS News poll: Talarico-Paxton Senate race is a Texas toss-up
summary: Turnout will be key as Texans voice cost of living concerns in Senate race between Ken Paxton and James Talarico.
story: The Texas Senate race is tight — essentially tied — and now all about...turnout.

Republican Ken Paxton benefits from the state's overall Republican leanings, while Democrat James Talarico is boosted by voters' economic concerns and higher perceptions of personal character to serve as senator.

Talarico's standing is helped by more Democrats saying they'll definitely vote. That leaves the dynamic in the closing weeks very much up for grabs. If more Republicans decide to vote, it could certainly change.
The bulk of Paxton's voters are backing him either because he's the GOP nominee or to oppose Talarico, and because they want to support President Trump.
Where Talarico does well

Some of the economic headwinds facing Republicans nationally are showing up here. The cost of living is the top issue for Texas voters, and most say they've been negatively affected by higher prices. Among these voters, Talarico enjoys a sizable lead over Paxton.
And more see Talarico as having the right character to serve as senator.
Personal qualities matter far more to Talarico's backers than to Paxton's.
Talarico gets 5% of those who identify as Republicans.
On a wider scale, he draws 9% of people who — regardless of their own party affiliation — say they never vote for Democrats, but will this time.
Where Paxton does well

But some things are different in Texas than in the country overall: The Trump administration's deportation program gets more support in Texas, compared to the most recent CBS News national poll, and that advantages Paxton.
And outside the economic considerations, Republicans say they feel Talarico represents policies that are a threat to their culture and way of life.
(Democrats, for their part, feel the same about Paxton.)
A lot of Paxton's backing from Republicans is an effort to support Trump.
And in a state where few voters describe themselves as liberal, Talarico is viewed as "very liberal" by nearly half. When they describe Talarico this way, they're voting for Paxton.
Demographics on vote

Texas just has a lot more Republicans than Democrats. That means Talarico needs to do overwhelmingly well with independents and get some vote shift among GOPers, or activate enough new voters to offset that.
He also needs strong turnout from younger voters, who today say they back him in large percentages. Historically, younger voters don't typically turn out at as high a rate as older voters do.

Latino voters in Texas swung toward Trump in 2024, but most are now backing Democrat Talarico. Latinos are more likely than voters overall to say higher prices have been a hardship or difficult, and most of them do not think Paxton has the right personal character to serve as a senator.
The race for governor
Incumbent Greg Abbott has an edge over Democrat Gina Hinojosa in the race for governor.
Abbott also receives the backing of 7% of Talarico voters.

This CBS News/YouGov survey was conducted with a representative sample of 1,492 registered voters in Texas  interviewed between October 8-16, 2026. The sample was weighted according to gender, age, race and education based on  U.S. Census data, as well as to 2024 presidential vote. The margin of error is ± 3.4 points for the sample of registered voters, and ± 3.5 points for likely voters.

title: Rep. Turner calls for congressional probe into Starlink disruption
summary: GOP Rep. Mike Turner of Ohio called for a congressional investigation into disruptions in Ukraine to satellite communications with Starlink, the technology owned by SpaceX's Elon Musk.
story: Washington — GOP Rep. Mike Turner of Ohio on Sunday called for a congressional investigation into disruptions in Ukraine to satellite communications with Starlink, the technology owned by SpaceX's Elon Musk.
"There needs to be an investigation, we need to find out who these people are because lives are at risk and lives are lost over these things," Turner said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

Last week, Ukrainian officials began reporting experiencing difficulties with the satellite communication system, which is used for communication and to control drones, prompting questions about who was behind the slowdown. President Trump said on Friday he had not limited Ukraine's access to Starlink, adding he didn't believe Musk was responsible either. On Saturday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that the administration had "nothing to do with that." Rubio said no one ordered the Starlink speed to be slowed, claiming it "sort of happened," while adding that it had been restored.
Turner said the explanation wasn't sufficient.
"This is something where there needs to be an investigation, there needs to be a congressional investigation," Turner said Sunday. "We need to find out who these people are."

On the technology, Turner said, "there are areas where it's restored, and there are areas where perhaps it is not," pointing to assessments in Ukraine, including from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Zelenskyy said Saturday that Ukraine is still unable to use its interceptor systems against Russian drones due to the Starlink speed restrictions.

"People's lives are at risk, and this is within Ukraine, this is areas where they're trying to defend themselves," Turner said. "This is essential to the United States' support of Ukraine in defending real aggressive attacks by Russia within Ukraine, and this needs to be restored."
GOP Sen. Kevin Cramer of North Dakota, who also appeared on "Face the Nation" on Sunday, also called for a congressional probe.

"I certainly support investigating what was the source of that decision, if in fact it was a decision at all," Cramer said. "It may very well have been some sort of a technical glitch, I don't know for sure."

Cramer added, "We want to get to the bottom of it." But in the meantime, he said "what's more important is that that power is put back on full scale, and that we actually enhance Ukraine's ability to hit these launch facilities inside of Russia."

The comments come after a bipartisan group of nine senators, including Republican Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, Susan Collins of Maine, John Cornyn of Texas and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, requested an inspector general investigation into the  slowdown last week.

In a letter to the Pentagon's inspector general, the group of senators, led by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, asked for the investigation into "whether actions or decisions by the Department of Defense or its contractors contributed to these dangerous circumstances."

"Any restrictions on these capabilities, particularly without advance notification, raise serious questions about the Department of Defense's contractual oversight and its responsibility to ensure continuity of essential services," the senators wrote.

title: Full transcript of "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 18, 2026
summary: On this "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" broadcast, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso join Margaret Brennan.
story: On this "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" broadcast, moderated by Margaret Brennan:

Anthony Salvanto, CBS News executive director of elections and surveys Rep. Mike Turner, Republican of Ohio Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon, Democratic candidate for Senate Sen. Kevin Cramer, Republican of North Dakota Anthony Salvanto, CBS News executive director of elections and surveys, Caitlin Huey Burns, CBS News political correspondent and Ed O'Keefe, CBS News senior White House and political correspondent

Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon, Democratic candidate for Senate

Click here to browse full transcripts from 2026 of "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
MARGARET BRENNAN: I'm Margaret Brennan in Washington.
And this week on Face the Nation: Midterm elections campaigning enters the homestretch, and President Trump's latest move to ease pressure on Vladimir Putin sparks fury among some Republicans.
From East to West and far North to Deep South, it's down to the sweet 16 for the 2026 candidates, even for the politician whose name won't actually appear on any ballot this year.
(Begin VT)
DONALD TRUMP (President of the United States): What an honor. I love doing this stuff, you know? This is worth the eight hours in a plane.
(LAUGHTER)
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: And don't forget, I got eight hours going back too.
(End VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: The president says his quest for a red state romp is working.
(Begin VT)

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: So I think these rallies have changed everything. I think a lot of people that maybe were having trouble won't have so much trouble. But I feel I owe it to the Republican Party.
(End VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: But will the rallies be enough to reverse those hurricane-force headwinds the president's party is facing? We have brand- new polling on that Texas race. It's one of the tightest toss-ups in the country.
Democrats face their own tough challenges, like getting a fractured party to go out and vote, if not for them, then against Trump's Republican candidate.
(Begin VT)
STATE REP. ANGIE NIXON (D-Florida) (Senatorial Candidate): Are you ready to put an end to corruption that's driving up our prices and ruining our democracy?
(CHEERING)
STATE REP. ANGIE NIXON: Well, I'm ready too.
(End VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: We will also look at the president's latest move to make it easier for Vladimir Putin to sell oil, an executive order freezing the just-passed Lindsey Graham law intended to cut off funding for Putin's war chest.
Ohio Republican Congressman Mike Turner and North Dakota Senator Kevin Cramer will weigh in on that. And we will talk with Florida Democratic Senate nominee Angie Nixon.
It's all just ahead on Face the Nation.
Good morning, and welcome to Face the Nation.

With just two weeks and two days until November 3, there is no better way to begin the broadcast today than with our executive director of elections and surveys, Anthony Salvanto, with our brand-new Texas poll.
Anthony, good morning.
CBS estimates Democrats have the edge to take the House. They need four seats to take the Senate. How can they do it?
ANTHONY SALVANTO: Well, you set the scene.

Through the fall, the Democrats have put a lot of Senate races in play in a lot of red Republican-leaning states. Texas is a really good example of that. So, let me take you there. What you have got here in the matchup between Talarico and Paxton, our new poll shows this really as tight as can be, Margaret, at 51-49.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Wow.
ANTHONY SALVANTO: But the story in there is a common theme that we see running through a lot of these races. One is, can the Republican base consolidate behind their candidates?

Here in Texas, you see, at least because they're the party's nominee is one reason that folks are backing Paxton. But at the same time, you also see a big thing here, where you have got these party breaks, Talarico doing better with independents and also better with people who say that they're hurting financially because of prices.

That's a common theme. And I'm going to take you back to the map now and show you the rest of these places that we're really watching, for one thing, Ohio. That's another state that the president won fairly easily. That, we see as a toss-up. I can take you out to Alaska. This is another toss-up, again, a Republican-leaning state.

And there are a couple of others too. To just remind folks, Iowa, it's leaning red right now in this race, but certainly competitive. Even Kansas is another spot that we're going to be watching closely on election night in that one. And, again, to remind folks, this is a place the president won easily, but is in play now.

So that's the Democrats' challenge that comes along with that expanded map. One other point, though, because it's really important as we go. You have got to watch for the Democrats to hold on to places that they already have.

So, Michigan, this is a toss-up. They'd have to hold up. And then another one, I'm going to show you, Maine, because this one's interesting, Susan Collins running for reelection in a state that Kamala Harris won. This race is neck-and-neck too, and that's a toss-up, probably also one the Democrats would have to have.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, the last time you were here, you told us Democratic voters were telling you they're more likely to show up at the polls than Republicans were. Is that still the case?
ANTHONY SALVANTO: It is. And I'm going to show you a slide that kind of tells the tale here.

This is from our House estimates. And you see this gap between the Democrats who say they're definitely going to vote and the Republicans who say they're definitely going to vote. This is driving a lot of the gaps you see in the polling, and it's also driving the political narrative, the president hitting the campaign trail, trying to boost that Republican turnout.
Because Republicans, especially if they say inflation has hit them hard, they're not going to vote for Democrats, but they might stay home.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And that's everything, turnout.
Anthony Salvanto, thank you.
ANTHONY SALVANTO: Thanks.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And we're joined now by Ohio Republican Congressman Mike Turner.
Good morning, and thanks for being here in person.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER (R-Ohio): Thank you.
(CROSSTALK)
MARGARET BRENNAN: A lot to get to with you, but let's start on politics.

Ohio has been reliably Republican, but you've got a competitive gubernatorial race and Senate race. In Minnesota, in Iowa, in Michigan, and in Maine, Republicans have been positioning themselves as independent of the president on some issues. Take a listen.
(Begin VT)
MICHELE TAFOYA (R-Minnesota Senatorial Candidate): When Trump is right, I will work with him. When he's wrong, I will stand up for Minnesota.

REPRESENTATIVE ASHLEY HINSON (R-Iowa) (Senatorial Candidate): We need to lower gas prices in this country. We need to lower diesel prices, but I don't think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it.
MIKE ROGERS (R-Michigan Senatorial Candidate): Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now.
SENATOR SUSAN COLLINS (R-Maine): I agree that the president did not have a good plan. He should have anticipated the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
(End VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: I know you've been endorsed by President Trump. You did appear at a rally with him, but do you feel it would help to create some distance, like they did?

REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Well, as you know, I don't run with the president. I don't run from the president. It's one of the reasons why you have me on this show, because of the fact that – that I have my – my own agenda.

And I think what's important, as your pollster has – has indicated, he's in – he's talking of – of trends. What's most important, as he ended his presentation, as Anthony said, this is about who gets out to vote, and everybody needs to get out and vote.

You know, Margaret, my very first race, I won by 244 votes out of 44,000. It's really, really important as to who gets out and votes. So, my message would be to everyone is to get out and vote. And also, when they go to the polls, they need to make certain that they vote in every race.
It's amazing the number of drop-offs…
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: … that people have. As they go down the ballot, people need to vote in every race, and they need to get out and vote.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But, clearly, those candidates felt they needed to say that.

FOX had a poll this week showing six in 10 respondents were extremely concerned about government corruption. AP had one that said six in 10 adults believe Trump is illegally profiting from the presidency or at least doing something unethical.

Your local paper, "The Columbus Dispatch," wrote it could not endorse the Republican Senate candidate because of the "abject failure" – this is a quote – "of Republicans in Congress to stop visible corruption and abuse of power by the Trump administration." They referred to Republicans as almost entirely spineless.
How do you counter those perceptions? Do you feel you need to?
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: No, first off, that – Columbus is not my local – local paper. And – and the…
MARGARET BRENNAN: You're Dayton.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Right, yes. I'm – I'm – I'm Dayton…
MARGARET BRENNAN: But it is still talking about the Senate race and talking about the perception that Congress has not pushed back on the president.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Right.

Well, I think – I think Congress has pushed back, and, certainly, I have pushed back. And in – in my community, I'm seen as part of the integral economic development team, the local economic development team of my community.

And the – the aspect of what people are doing or are not doing with respect to this administration is, I think, an individual candidate's issue. And people vote for individual candidates. They don't vote for a team. They don't vote for – for a slate.

And – and I think that's why individual candidates are talking about their individual records, as – as I do. People look in my community. They see me as a job creator. They see me as someone, if – Margaret, if you came into my community and we took a drive along my community, and I showed you my accomplishments, you'd see things at, you know, my local base, where we've doubled the jobs both inside and outside the fence, the VA, where we've created senior housing.
And, like, my opponent wouldn't be able to get out of the driveway of her house. Those are the kind of things that people look to for the individual candidates.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But the president is central here. The president is telling people, vote like he is on the ballot.
REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Well, that's – that's – that's the president. That's not the individual candidates.
MARGARET BRENNAN: He thinks he's doing candidates like you some – some good when he says things like that and comes out and rallies in Ohio.

SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER: So, that – you're right, that was a proposal we brought to President Zelenskyy. SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER: While President Zelenskyy has simply gone after, you know, the launchers and, more importantly, these – you know, the war machine's funding source, which is energy.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

MARGARET BRENNAN: And that's what he means when he says, vote like I'm on the ballot.
ED O'KEEFE: Yes. Yes. It's –

MARGARET BRENNAN: I also, in this poll, was struck, 59 percent of likely voters told Anthony Ken Paxton does not have the right personal character to serve as senator. 45 percent said Talerico does not. Does that match what both of you have heard on the ground?
ED O'KEEFE: I think so. I mean – you go ahead.

CAITLIN HUEY-BURNS: Yes. Absolutely. I mean I was in Texas last week, and, I mean, this is why the president went there three times in the span of nearly three weeks, because he has to pull Paxton over the finish line. He's wildly unpopular.

But when it comes to Texas, the thing that I've been saying is, everything has to go wrong for Republicans and exactly right for Democrats in order to win there. So, it's not just enough that people don't like Paxton and depressing the Republican vote, it's also that you have to turn out those independents and convert voters to the Democratic side in a deep red state. Talerico is going to have to build a coalition that no Democrat has been able to do in over 30 years. It's a tall order.

ED O'KEEFE: I will say, we were there first in March when the primaries were held and Talerico was already on this, focus on corruption, which I think we've seen Democrats everything else, especially in the last few weeks, really begin to pick up on, such that it's starting to show up in polling –
MARGARET BRENNAN: For the president or for Paxton, who has faced allegations?
ED O'KEEFE: For everyone. But in the – but in that case specific, he was linking Paxton and Trump together.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Got it.

ED O'KEEFE: Emphasis on Paxton ahead of the general. And now you see Democrats across the country focused on corruption, either against the president or the Republican they're running against or, you know, the governor in that state. So, he was, in essence, a leading indictor, or, you know, he saw something coming with the uniquely unpopular candidate that he has that other Democrats have not been able to pick on, with all the examples we've seen across the country.

You say they've got to pull off a miracle in Texas. Democrats need to pull off at least four miracles on election night across the country in states where they've never done it before. That's what makes this such a high bar for them to reach on election night.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I want to ask you about Michigan.
ED O'KEEFE: Yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I know you were just there. I like your vote bracelet, by the way.
ED O'KEEFE: This was made by my daughter. Yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Very cute.
ED O'KEEFE: Get out and vote.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You – the president talks about this race all the time.
ED O'KEEFE: Yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Specifically the Democratic candidate there who would be, if he wins, the first Muslim senator to ever sit in Congress. This was one of President Trump's latest remarks.
(BEGIN VC)
DONALD TRUMP, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: You have a jihadist running in Michigan. He's not like leaning left. He was so far left, there is no such thing as the word. This guy's a jihadist.
(END VC)
MARGARET BRENNAN: Abdul El-Sayed, how is he handling that kind of rhetoric, which is basically accusing him of being a terrorist, and is the Republican candidate comfortable with this?

ED O'KEEFE: Well, he's repeating it himself. We saw him give a speech this week just ahead of the vice president on Thursday in the Detroit area where he spent about 90 percent of his speech laying out accusations similar to what the president is suggesting, that he has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, that he's too extreme for Michigan, that he hasn't denounced the IRGC and thinks that Israel's a bigger threat than Iran.

El-Sayed has, in various ways, addressed this by saying, first of all, no, he has no associations with the Muslim Brotherhood. He was asked by a voter, does he disavow them? The answer was "yes." It was followed by a long respond targeting that person for raising it at all and suggesting that the only reason Republicans are doing this is because he's Muslim or Arab and is different. He ties himself to the legacies of John F. Kennedy and Barack Obama in being firsts. But the difference was, Kennedy and Obama, I'd argue, went out and sort of proactively addressed the fact that they would be historic and different in speeches.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
ED O'KEEFE: And did it in a – in a – I guess a more positive way. El- Sayed continues to sort of raise it, or answer questions about it and then accuse people of being – why would you raise that?
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
ED O'KEEFE: Well, he's the one raising it to some extent by pointing out the history of it. But then when people ask these questions, it gets quite defensive and aggressive about it.

The thing is, he's anticipating that voters in Michigan are more upset about the economy, more upset about the war, less concerned about him. It is quite the gamble. And one that he continues to say he's going to win by seven percent. I don't think the polls show that. But he's standing by about to win by seven percent. We'll see.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Just quickly on Michigan. You interviewed Mike Rogers and you asked him about his wife handing out $10 cards to go buy gas.
ED O'KEEFE: Yes. Yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Is that legal?

ED O'KEEFE: Well, buying votes is not legal, no. And I asked Rogers, what was your wife doing there? And he said, well, she paid for these out-of- pocket and she was trying to raise awareness about our campaign.
MARGARET BRENNAN: How does that make a difference?
ED O'KEEFE: I – that was his answer when I asked, right?
MARGARET BRENNAN: OK.

ED O'KEEFE: I mean you saw – this was on social media. People caught this. But he also made the point that she was doing this in black areas of Detroit. He has made a concerted effort to reach out to black voters in that city, believing that there is softness for El-Sayed, and the polling suggests there is. And certainly what we heard this week suggests that he still has work to do there. But Rogers is trying to make inroads there. Handing out gift cards, meeting with pastors. He told me at one point that he met a black pastor who, in his 70 years that that church had existed, no Republican office holder or politician had ever shown up.
MARGARET BRENNAN: OK.
ED O'KEEFE: That might work on the margins in close races. We'll see.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Caitlin, you have spent some time in Kansas. President Trump's heading there.
CAITLIN HUEY-BURNS: Yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We were just talking about beef prices with the North Dakota senator.
CAITLIN HUEY-BURNS: Yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: This is a problem for Roger Marshall in Kansas.

CAITLIN HUEY-BURNS: I mean I was there a couple weeks ago, not a place I expected to be in the final stretch of this campaign. No Democrat has won the Senate race in Kansas since 1932. That's nearly a century.

But there's a lot at place here that I think speaks to the broader themes of this election. First of all, kind of going back to the point I made, Roger Marshall is a candidate – a current incumbent that Republicans kind of feel meh about. They like the president, but not necessarily translating to him. Everything you've been seeing across the country, the cost of diesel, especially for farmers in Kansas, is important.

But I spent an afternoon with a cattle farmer in Kansas who likes the president, supported the president, time and again, still supports him, but the decision that the administration made to allow beef imports into the market, that is something that is directly affecting him. And he told me, for the first time he is considering voting for the Democrat Adam Hamilton here, who I interviewed, and he said, you know, if you talk to him, he often references that he's a former Republican, he's not campaigning on the national party brand, which he can't do in a place like Kansas.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

CAITLIN HUEY-BURNS: But he's making it competitive because of kind of that perfect storm of complications that Republicans have going for them. And then the nuances in a lot of these races. Administration policies directly affecting the constituencies that tend to vote for Trump. So, that gets to the turnout question.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.
CAITLIN HUEY-BURNS: Is that enough to depress them and enough to convert a couple of them?
MARGARET BRENNAN: And that, Anthony, is what you're going to be focused on basically all night on November 3rd.
ANTHONY SALVANTO: Yes. Well, look, this national context, to Caitlin's point, is neither party not only is viewed favorably, but neither one is viewed by most as able to help you financially.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

ANTHONY SALVANTO: And that's important because, yes, is speaks to localized races or state-specific races, in many cases that Democrats would like this to be all nationalized because, on the national level, there is that opposition to the administration's policies.

But, at the same time, when you talk about who owns the economy and you ask that, it is the Trump administration in the minds of most, because of those policies, because of the war, and because of gas prices.
MARGARET BRENNAN: OK.
Very quickly, Caitlin, any word on who's behind these 36 lawmakers receiving threatening envelopes?

CAITLIN HUEY-BURNS: Yes, suspicious substances, a lot of them intercepted before they reached Capitol Hill offices. But not only for U.S. senators and lawmakers, but also for election officials, which is really startling. It's been 25 years since the anthrax issue after 9/11. And what is really especially jarring is, they don't – they haven't released who – or talked about who may be behind this. Federal law enforcement is investigating. But the uptick that we've seen and threats against lawmakers and their families has risen in the past year over 50 percent.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes. Yes, it's something we are tracking very much in our public life these days.
Thank you all for this panel.
ED O'KEEFE: Good to see you.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Get ready, it's going to be a fun two weeks.
CAITLIN HUEY-BURNS: Buckle up.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We'll be back in a moment.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's it for us today. We'll see you next week.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)

title: Ukraine, Sudan immigrants to retain deportation protections for now
summary: The TPS protections of tens of thousands of Ukrainians and hundreds of Sudanese immigrants were officially slated to terminate on Monday.
story: Immigrants from Ukraine and Sudan enrolled in the Temporary Protected Status policy will be able to live and work in the U.S. without fear of deportation for the time being, even though their protections were set to expire soon, the Department of Homeland Security told CBS News on Sunday.
The TPS protections of tens of thousands of Ukrainians and hundreds of Sudanese immigrants were officially slated to terminate on Monday.
But in statements on Sunday, DHS said final decisions on the fate of the humanitarian immigration programs will "be made at the appropriate time."
Until such decisions are announced, DHS added, nationals of Ukraine and Sudan enrolled in the TPS program will "retain protection."
The decisions to keep the deportation protections in place, albeit not final, stand in sharp contrast to the Trump administration's broader posture toward TPS programs.

Trump administration officials have routinely denounced TPS as a de facto amnesty policy abused by the Biden administration that encourages illegal immigration and that has been extended too often, despite its temporary nature.

Over the past year and a half, the Trump administration, as part of its aggressive immigration crackdown, has revoked the TPS protections of more than 1 million immigrants from over a dozen countries, including Afghanistan, Haiti and Venezuela.

The programs for Ukrainian and Sudanese nationals are among a handful of TPS policies that have remained in place nearly two years into President Trump's second term, alongside the protections for tens of thousands of immigrants from El Salvador. Their TPS program was also set to lapse last month, but DHS retained their protections, pending a final announcement.

Created in 1990 by Congress, TPS allows the U.S. government to offer a temporary deportation reprieve and work permits to immigrants, illegal and legal alike, who hail from countries facing armed conflict, an environmental disaster or another crisis that makes their return there unsafe.

The TPS policy for Ukrainians was first announced by the Biden administration in the spring of 2022, soon after Russia launched its full-blown invasion of Ukraine. As of March 2025, there were more than 100,000 Ukrainians enrolled in TPS, including those allowed into the U.S. under a Biden-era sponsorship policy.

The TPS program for Sudan has been around since the late 1990s, with different administrations extending the policy due to the armed conflict and political turmoil that has plagued the African nation. As of March 2025, roughly 1,800 Sudanese nationals had TPS.
This story published first on CBS News at 1:44 p.m. on Oct. 18, 2026.

title: Trump says D.C. golf course construction will start next month
summary: President Trump said Sunday that construction at the historic East Potomac Golf Links course will begin Nov. 15.
story: President Trump said Sunday that construction on a historic Washington, D.C., golf course will begin next month, despite an ongoing court challenge to his long-sought renovation of the East Potomac Golf Links course.

"I am pleased to announce that the Department of the Interior, under the auspices of Secretary Doug Burgum, and in conjunction with famed Golf Course Architect, Tom Fazio, has developed a plan to build a World Class Championship Golf Course on the site of the current East Potomac Golf Links, located in Washington, D.C.," Mr. Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.

The president, who did not acknowledge the court challenge in his post, said that while the new golf course would remain open to the public, it would also be designed to host tournaments like the U.S. Open, the PGA Championship, the Ryder Cup and the Presidents Cup. He also billed it as a "tremendously positive" economic opportunity for D.C. that would "create many jobs."

Mr. Trump described the current course as an "old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect ... with falling, dangerous, and disease infested trees, and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall." He said the site "was famous for no trees" originally but has since become "overgrown, dysfunctional, and unsafe."
Mr. Trump said construction will begin Nov. 15 on the course, which will be closed for about 15 months until the new one opens.

His announcement Sunday came less than a week after a federal judge barred the Trump administration from removing trees at the current golf course through Oct. 16, after hundreds of trees were cut down the weekend prior.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes said in the order that until that date, the administration may not make "any irreparable modification" to the East Potomac course without first providing three business days' notice of such plans to the court, as well as to the plaintiffs in a lawsuit seeking to stop Mr. Trump's planned overhaul of the site.

"The administration has time and again tried to avoid the law in their mad rush toward converting a public recreation space to a high-end golf course and today's order will stop them from doing further irreparable harm to a precious public resource," said attorneys for the plaintiffs, the D.C. Preservation League and two local golfers, in response to the judge's order. "We are pleased that the court intervened and will prevent additional work while we seek more lasting relief."

title: Book excerpt: "Your Turn: How to Create a Midlife You Love"
summary: NPR health and science correspondent and "Sunday Morning" contributor Allison Aubrey writes about the steps Gen Xers may take to foster a sense of purpose as they enter this next stage of life.
story: We may receive an affiliate commission from anything you buy from this article.

In "Your Turn: How to Create a Midlife You Love" (Avid Reader Press/Simon & Schuster), NPR health and science correspondent and "Sunday Morning" contributor Allison Aubrey writes about the steps Gen Xers may take to foster a sense of purpose as they enter this next stage of life.
Read the excerpt below, and don't miss Allison Aubrey's commentary on "CBS Sunday Morning" October 18!
Prefer to listen? Audible has a 30-day free trial available right now.

If you've been so busy taking care of others that you haven't had time for yourself, you're not alone. As a Gen X woman, I've spent decades in the trenches, toggling between kids and career. When I hit a midlife wall, I took a sabbatical from my day job. I called it a "curiosity tour," and I went in search of people making bold, heartfelt pivots. What I found made me excited for the future. These women showed me how much opportunity and adventure can still lie ahead.

One way to start a midlife reset is to make time to be creative. Creativity lets us express what's inside of us, and it can be a bridge to connection. Sometimes the nudge to begin comes from someone else's story.
Excerpt from Chapter 8, It's About Damn Time
"I used to be so delusional. I always imagined I could be more than I was, and eventually I grew and evolved into that person." —Lady Gaga

Every spring, I take a bluebell hike with my friends, when the purplish bell-shaped wildflowers temporarily blanket the woodlands along the Potomac River. Last year, Amy Wilton, a friend of a friend who happens to be a professional photographer, joined us. When the hike was over, as she scrolled through to share her images, it wasn't the bluebells I found engaging. "Wait, stop, go back," I said as she flitted through.
It was a portrait she'd taken in Maine that caught my eye, of a woman singing onstage. A picture can paint a thousand words, but this one painted one: transcendence. I had to know more.

I visited Kristi Kalajian in Camden, Maine, where she lives. Turns out, Kristi works as a PA, a physician assistant. Her part-time gig is as a singer in a band, a role she didn't seriously entertain until her fiftieth birthday.

Kristi has a lush and smoky voice and has always loved R&B. As her fiftieth birthday approached, that I need to sing feeling resurfaced. She made up a set list of her favorite songs and began practicing to get her voice back into shape. "I was so nervous," Kristi told me. She invited a bunch of people to the home of a friend, who had a gorgeous grand piano. The concert was a runaway success.

So, what next? She didn't want to stop. She really wanted to be in a band again. "Looking back, that was definitely the thing that was missing in my life," she says. But she lives in a small town and had two teenagers at the time, as well as her job that required long hours, so road shows were a nonstarter.

Maybe it was just a dream. Time passed. Then, she was invited to a New Year's celebration where the host asked everyone to make a vision board. Kristi had always considered this kind of thing to be hokey, but she went along anyway. Throwing caution and cynicism to the wind, she picked up a pair of scissors and, without thinking, began to cut out pictures of musicians and instruments, a band and horn players, and, yes, a singer performing to a cheering crowd.

Not more than a month later, a local musician approached her. "Hey, a friend is looking for a singer with a smoky voice to join his band. Interested?" Within a few weeks, they were rehearsing, and they've been playing gigs ever since.
When Kristi stepped up to sing the lead on her band's rendition of Lizzo's 2020 hit song, "About Damn Time," I couldn't help thinking that she had found her third-turn anthem.

The great thing about the third turn is that we don't need to "adult" all the time anymore, as parenting and workloads lighten, and our creative spirits can come out to play. According to Dr. Jeremy Nobel, a primary care doctor and poet, the formula is simple: "Be curious. Make things. Have conversations."
Kristi, now in her sixties, has experienced moments of self-doubt. "Sing Lizzo, at my age?" But she has learned to override the doubt. "I feel complete," she told me.

If she had waited until she had retired from her job, this moment might never have come. Even if it's dipping your toe in the water, taking the first step is essential. After dozens of interviews, I'm convinced there's an art form for everyone. If it's not calling you yet, here are some tips to get started.

Try one thing. There are so many creative pursuits—painting, pottery, poetry, music, theater, culinary arts, and gardening (which Nobel calls the "slowest form of performance art"). Just pick one—there's no pressure. If you don't like it, try something else. That's part of the pleasure of creativity in midlife. For more inspiration, check out the CreativityHub, which is full of prompts to get your creative juices flowing.

How were you creative as a child? Creativity comes easily to children, so think back to when you found joy in making something, or singing or dancing, or just pretending (i.e., creating stories). Katy Baytosh loves to dance. Turn on the music, and this buttoned-down college admissions advisor is transformed back into her teenage diva self! She teaches Shake Your Soul classes. "It's a way for people to tap into the creative spirit without thinking about it as a performance," Baytosh says. You're not competing to be the most graceful or the best. "It's about heartfelt expression through connecting to yourself and others." When I took Katy's class, it had been eons since I'd danced as if no one was watching (and thank God they were not!). Look for opportunities to try rekindling creative practices from your childhood. Find a class or a group that shares your passion. Remember, there's no trophy. It's just about joy and connection. You're trading performance for pleasure.

Start a group to share creative prompts. For some people, creativity is also a way to maintain friendships. One of my former colleagues, Alison Richards, remains close with three friends from England, where she grew up. These women live on different continents, and their IRL meetups are rare, so they started a WhatsApp group. It's a place to share ideas and generate inspiration. They all work with the same prompt, say a nature photo or a line of prose. Then each woman takes it in her own direction. One may write a poem, while another paints or sings about it. The beauty of this practice is that it nurtures both creativity and connection.

title: California's proposed billionaire tax: How does it add up?
summary: California voters will decide whether to adopt Proposition 40, which would impose a new tax on billionaires' wealth. "Sunday Morning" examines whether the measure would deliver the benefits its backers promise — and why some progressives oppose it.
story: When California voters head to the polls next month, they'll be asked whether to adopt a new proposal that calls for billionaires to be taxed like never before. Jo Ling Kent shares what Proposition 40 is all about:
"There's never been a proposal like this anywhere in the world, so it's a novel idea," said healthcare workers union leader Dave Regan. "We are facing an emergency."
An emergency that began, according to Regan, with President Trump's so-called "One Big Beautiful Bill," which includes cuts targeting federal funds to Medicaid over the next few years.

"What we're trying to do is restore $100 billion worth of health care cuts," Regan said. "Three-and-a-half million people lose health insurance. Hospitals, clinics, and emergency rooms will close." They could also cost jobs in Regan's own union, SEIU United Healthcare Workers West.

So, to bridge the gap, Regan and the union led a petition drive to put on the November ballot a one-time, 5% state tax on the net worth of California's 200 or so billionaires, known as Proposition 40.
How confident is Regan that it will pass? "Pretty confident," he replied.

Regan's tactics are controversial. His behavior? Under scrutiny. But if the wealth tax passes, he expects the state will collect $100 billion over five years, with 90% specifically earmarked for healthcare.

"We're not trying to pretend that it's a permanent solution," Regan said, "but a five-year solution is better than no solution. And that gives the state of California an opportunity to figure out what's the right permanent solution."
Asked if a five-year tax is a solution, Regan replied, "Absolutely. Ask the three-and-a-half million people who are going to lose healthcare coverage."
Competing Propositions

Since the wealth tax was proposed, some billionaires have left California, including venture capitalist Peter Thiel, and Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin. Brin is spending more than $100 million to oppose the measure.

And California being California, there are two other opposition-backed proposals on the ballot, Propositions 41 and 42. If either one receives more votes than Prop 40, that effectively nullifies the wealth tax.

And the billionaires have some strange bedfellows: several other major unions and big-name Democrats agree with them on voting no, including California Governor Gavin Newsom (who calls Prop 40 "a flawed initiative"), and former Democratic Congresswoman Katie Porter.

"I generally, as a progressive, have fought to make sure that the ultra-wealthy pay more," Porter said. "But this tax doesn't do that correctly, causing these people to pick up and to leave. We want billionaires to create jobs here, to start companies here. …

"You don't get a second bite at tax policy," she continued. "A tax that you pass has enduring consequences. When somebody leaves California, we can no longer tax them. That is a permanent problem. It is much harder to get tax base back than it is to grow it in the first place."

Here's where taxes get complicated: billionaires can pay a lot in income, property and capital gains taxes. But most of their wealth is typically growing in stocks, which aren't taxed until they sell.

"It's a system in which essentially the richest Americans have been written out of the tax system, much like the aristocracy of pre-revolutionary France," said Ray Madoff, a professor at Boston College Law. "People who have enough money to live on their investments and inheritances legally don't have to pay any taxes."

Madoff says Prop 40 spotlights a "deeply broken" tax system, and believes it can be beneficial. "My feelings about Prop 40 are that meaningful change has to happen at the federal level," she said. "And I think that to the extent Prop 40 creates an incentive for meaningful change to take effect on the federal level, then I'd say it would be helpful. On its own, it obviously can't do anything; it's just patching a temporary hole, right? But I think that there is a certain amount of symbolic value of Prop 40."
"California is America's coming attraction"
As for how this turns out, the polls are tightening, with voters now more divided. A "Yes" voter told us, "To me, it's bigger than Prop 40. It's a fight back against the Trump administration."
A "No" voter said, "We really are concerned about people leaving the state."

No billionaires contacted by "Sunday Morning" wanted to talk to us about Prop 40 … except for one. "I don't mind paying taxes; the more you make, the more taxes you pay, so I'm okay with that," said Jensen Huang, the founder and CEO of the American chipmaker Nvidia, headquartered in Silicon Valley. "I don't like tax dollars wasted. But I also support all that this country represents."
Huang's first job was as a dishwasher at Denny's. Today, Forbes lists his net worth at about $200 billion, making him the seventh richest person in the world.

"I am the ultimate American dream," Huang said. "If not for this country, the education, the ability to create a new company, pursue your dreams, I wouldn't have met all the people that made Nvidia possible. I love this country in every possible way. And it's not perfect, but it's incredible."

Even if you end up paying perhaps $8 billion over five years? "The fact that I can afford to pay $8 billion in taxes over five years is a privilege," Huang replied. "I'm not afraid of paying taxes. I'm just afraid of being poor."

Whether you're poor or rich, for or against the billionaire tax, its architect, Dave Regan, is already looking beyond November – and beyond California. "Other states around the country are going to start looking to follow California's lead, just like it's happened so many times in the past," he said. "California is America's coming attraction, and this is coming to a state near you after we pass it on November 3."
Story produced by Dustin Stephens. Editor: Emanuele Secci.
