title: Elusive murder suspect falls victim to detectives' chewing gum sting
summary: A detective from Everett, Washington, linked two cold case killings to a known predator. Needing fresh DNA to charge him, she helped devise a clever undercover sting using chewing gum to crack the case.
story: Detective Susan Logothetti lives her professional life deep in the past, investigating cold cases at the Everett Police Department, north of Seattle.
Det. Susan Logothetti: I love that people who thought they could get away with it 40 years ago are looking over their shoulder now, wondering what they left behind.
One case in particular from 1984 came to consume her: the killing of Judy Weaver, 42, a divorced mother and a manager of a bar and cafe.
Det. Susan Logothetti: It was called the Bel-Nes Cafe. … one of the roughest bars on Hewitt Avenue, if not the roughest.
The murder of Judy Weaver
Judy Weaver was beloved by her rowdy regulars for her generous shots of hard liquor and for being a little rough around the edges herself.
Det. Susan Logothetti: She could stand up to anybody.
The former local beauty queen could turn ugly when it came to dealing with intoxicated patrons, says her daughter, Cathy Myers.
Cathy Myers: … she'd just throw them out.
Peter Van Sant: What, grab them by the collar and you're out of here?
Cathy Myers: … by the back of the neck, back of the pants.
Peter Van Sant (looking at family photos): This is the beauty queen? …
Cathy Myers: This is our mom when she was the Salmon Derby Queen …
Colleen Kayser: … uh, she was a good mom.
Judy's other daughter, Colleen Kayser.
Colleen Kayser: She worked hard to make sure us girls had what … we needed.
For years, it was just the three of them  —  Colleen, Cathy, and their mom. But all that changed when Judy started dating the owner of the bar, Bill Richards.
Cathy Myers (pointing at photo): This is Bill Richards, my mom's boyfriend.
They eventually got engaged. Judy's daughters didn't like him very much.
Colleen Kayser: He didn't treat my mom very well. … Well, he was mean to her. He'd yell at her. He hit her a few times.
Peter Van Sant: Did you witness that?
Colleen Kayser: I never witnessed it, but I've seen the bruises.
Wanting a fresh start, on the evening of June 1, 1984, Bill and Judy popped some champagne.
Det. Susan Logothetti: They were celebrating the sale of the Bel-Nes. … they were there with friends, and they were partying. … Judy, she got pretty tipsy that night.

Too tipsy to drive and too tired to wait for a cab, Judy decided to walk home leaving Bill at the bar. Their apartment was about a half mile away. At some point, along the darkened streets, Judy was spotted and followed.
Det. Susan Logothetti: … this is where Judy Weaver would have walked to, to come home. That last door you see down here …
Det. Susan Logothetti: Judy likely left the back door unlocked when she came home.
Peter Van Sant: She goes inside. What do you believe happens next?
Det. Susan Logothetti: He … comes, finds the door unlocked and enters and attacks Judy.
About an hour later, says Logothetti, a neighbor saw smoke billowing out of Judy Weaver's apartment.
Peter Van Sant: When firefighters enter that apartment, what did they find? …
Det. Susan Logothetti: The bedroom door was closed. When they opened it, it was filled with black smoke.
Inside the smoldering bedroom was Judy Weaver,  tied up and motionless.
Det. Susan Logothetti: … she was obviously deceased.
Peter Van Sant: Why do you suppose the suspect set this fire?
Det. Susan Logothetti: To cover up the evidence and destroy the scene.
Logothetti spent hours examining the physical evidence: the silent witnesses to murder.
Det. Susan Logothetti: This was a pillowcase found next to Judy Weaver's body, and it's believed that it was covering her head. There's blood on it …
Det. Susan Logothetti: … her clothes had been cut with a knife …
Det. Susan Logothetti: It just looks like he did one straight shot …
Peter Van Sant: … cutting all along this line you can see.
Det. Susan Logothetti: In one straightened line.
Peter Van Sant: And then up here.
Det. Susan Logothetti: Because she didn't have cuts on her body, I feel like he took his time doing this …
Peter Van Sant: Drawing out the terror, right.
Det. Susan Logothetti: Yes.
Peter Van Sant: And what did that suggest about the assailant, someone who somehow took pleasure in inflicting this kind of pain and ultimately, death?
Det. Susan Logothetti: He's a monster. And I didn't believe that he hadn't done it before.
Judy Weaver was bound, sexually assaulted, and strangled.

Cathy Myers: I was told that her hands were tied and at that moment was when I, you know, took a second for that to sink in what that meant … and I instantly thought of Bill. And out loud I said, "Oh, my God, he killed her this time."
Other men were questioned, but it was Judy Weaver's fiancé, Bill Richards, who emerged as the prime suspect.
Cathy Myers: My only suspect was Bill …
But there was not enough evidence to charge him or to clear him. Bill Richards died in 1994 still a suspected murderer.
Det. Susan Logothetti: He was the prime suspect for 40 years …
In January 2023, this coldest of cold cases got another look. Logothetti says her boss back then believed recent advances in DNA technology might finally identify Judy Weaver's killer.
Det. Susan Logothetti: He … told me that it was likely Bill Richards, but he sent in evidence just to confirm it.
Months later, the DNA results landed on Logothetti's desk revealing a match and a name. To her surprise, that name was not Bill Richards.
DNA points to new suspect with a violent past
Detective Logothetti hoped a four-decade-long mystery was about to be solved. In the Judy Weaver cold case there was a DNA hit.
Peter Van Sant: And with that hit comes a name.
Det. Susan Logothetti: Yes.
Peter Van Sant: What name appeared?
Det. Susan Logothetti: Mitchell Allen Gaff.
A name she had never heard.
Det. Susan Logothetti: I immediately did a routine name check and the first thing I see is Mitchell Allen Gaff is a Level 3 registered sex offender and a sexually violent predator.
Peter Van Sant: What does a Level 3 offender mean?
Det. Susan Logothetti: They are the most likely to reoffend.
Detective Logothetti pored over Mitchell Gaff's case file. He was a free man after decades of incarceration for ultraviolent sexual assaults. His first known target: Jackie Brown.
Det. Susan Logothetti: She was a young police officer … beautiful woman, mowing her lawn and … caught Gaff's eye.
Peter Van Sant: He was just out walking in her neighborhood, right?
Det. Susan Logothetti: … he was.
It was the day before Thanksgiving 1979.
Peter Van Sant: You were in this very spot. Where are we right now?
Jackie Brown: We're in the backyard of my house …
Jackie Brown: I had just finished mowing the backyard …
Peter Van Sant: You're in your garage putting the lawnmower away.  What happens?
Jackie Brown (standing inside her garage): I heard someone yell, "Get down on your knees and don't turn around."
Jackie Brown: Of course I turned around.
Peter Van Sant: And is he standing right about where I am?
Jackie Brown: He's standing right about here.
A young man, she says, was pointing a gun just inches from her head.
Jackie Brown: He took the gun and slammed it across the side of my head. …
Jackie Brown: He kept hitting me. …
Jackie Brown: … he kept kneeing me …
Jackie Brown: And I thought, "He's going to rape me." And … I just kept talking. I said —
Talking, pleading and plotting. Jackie tried and failed to coax him out of the garage and into her bedroom.
Jackie Brown: Because I slept with a .38 caliber Smith & Wesson under my pillow. … and I knew … I'd blow his brains out. And I would have. …
Jackie Brown: And then he said, "put your hands behind your back."
In that whirlwind of fear, a childhood memory came rushing back, says Jackie. A lesson from her father: if attacked, fight like hell.
Jackie Brown: And he would say, "Well, fight, fight. Kick me. What are you doing to do? … fight dirty if you have to."
When the assailant put down the gun to handcuff Jackie, she turned her father's advice into action.
Jackie Brown: And I just threw my weight into him … caught him off guard and he fell against the wall. …
Jackie Brown: And he said, "I'm gonna kill you, you f****** bitch."
Jackie Brown: … all of a sudden he pulled out a hunting knife … And he slashed me …
Peter Van Sant: Where'd he slash you?
Jackie Brown: Across my left palm.
Jackie Brown: … and again, I shoved him, and I just ran out of the garage.
Jackie Brown: … and I sprint down the alley …
Peter Van Sant: … are you thinking he's right behind you?
Jackie Brown: Absolutely, yes. … I was screaming for help.
Jackie Brown: So, I'm flying down the middle of the road  …
A neighbor heard the commotion and called police. It wasn't long before Everett P.D. officers detained a man down by the railroad tracks, not far away. They needed Jackie to identify him.
Jackie Brown: … when we pulled up, I looked and … we were this far away. And I said, "That's not him." … he wasn't wearing anything that I described.
Peter Van Sant: So, you're thinking they got the wrong guy.
Jackie Brown: They got the wrong guy. Yep.
She started to leave, but something inside Jackie caused her to turn around.
Jackie Brown: And I – I said, "Say something to me." And I said it again really loud and he turned and he said, 'What the f*** do you want me to say?" And as soon as he said that I knew it was him.
Peter Van Sant: Wow.
Jackie Brown: I lunged for him.
Peter Van Sant: You lunged for him?
Jackie Brown: I lunged for him.

Her attacker – then 21-year-old Mitchell Gaff – was arrested.  Police later found his duffle bag, which contained the clothes he had worn during the attack. Gaff was convicted of assault with a deadly weapon. But, as a first-time offender, he was sentenced to one year of work release and five years of probation.
Peter Van Sant: What was that like for you to know he was out on the street?
Jackie Brown: Awful, awful. He got to carry on with his life, and it changed mine forever.

Combing through the case file, Logothetti began connecting the dots. She realized that Mitchell Gaff was still on probation for the Jackie Brown assault when Judy Weaver was murdered in June 1984. By the end of August, Gaff struck again.
Det. Susan Logothetti: … this house right here, is the house where the teenage sisters, Angela and Myra, were attacked and assaulted by Mitchell Gaff in August of 1984.
Det. Susan Logothetti: Angela was 14. Myra was 16.
It was close to midnight. They were both asleep: Angela on the living room couch … Myra down the hall in her bedroom …
Det. Susan Logothetti: … the front door was unlocked …
Mitchell Gaff slowly, silently, crept into the house, says Logothetti, collecting cords for ligatures and a knife from the kitchen.
Det. Susan Logothetti: After he found the items he wanted, in —   within the home, he went to Angela first.
Angela: … he grabbed me by my hair and pushed my head back and had a knife to my throat and said if you scream, I'm going to slit your throat.
In a 1996 interview on "60 Minutes Australia," Angela and Myra, then 27 and 29, relived the most terrifying two-and-a-half hours of their lives.
Myra: … some cloth was shoved all the way down my throat, and a gag was put on, and a pillowcase thrown over my head.
And then, Mitchell Gaff tied up the teenage sisters.
Det. Susan Logothetti: … and he proceeds to rape each of them …
Peter Van Sant: Was it headed toward a killing then of two young girls?
Det. Susan Logothetti: One hundred percent. … He grabs a blow dryer and uses the cord to strangle Angela.
Myra: … but he's choking her, right? He's killing her and it's my belief that he's going to kill her. And my reaction was to protect her, of course.
Myra took her free leg and started kicking him and screaming.
Myra: … he lost control and came over and just beat me to a pulp. …
Angela: He went over to start hitting her, and I just all the sudden got up. Got up and just took off out the door.
Peter Van Sant: She comes out of that front door. She's sprinting. Where does she go? …
Det. Susan Logothetti: She comes right over here to this house, her neighbor's house over here.
That gave Angela time to run for help …
Angela: I was naked. … and I ran acr —  down my yard all the way through, across the street to the next-door neighbor …
Det. Susan Logothetti: She couldn't understand why she couldn't scream. And she realized that this blow-dryer cord was still wrapped tightly, knotted around her neck. So, she took the blow dryer …
Angela: … and started hitting their door with the blow dryer that was around my neck.
Peter Van Sant: And what does Angela shout?
Det. Susan Logothetti: "He's killing Myra. He's killing Myra."
Horrified neighbors called police.
Det. Susan Logothetti: … and turned just in time to see Gaff run out the front door … fully naked … and run off into the darkness.
Myra and Angela had saved each other.

Mitchell Gaff was arrested about a week later in September 1984. Married with a pregnant wife, Gaff was convicted of aggravated rape and served 10 years in prison. Considered too dangerous to release, he was sent to McNeil Island in Washington for therapeutic treatment, and, possibly, indefinite civil detention.
Tom Junod: The only way that these guys could get out was to convince people that they were no longer a threat.

Tom Junod has authored dozens of acclaimed articles and written his first book, a memoir. In 1995, he profiled Mitchell Gaff for GQ Magazine. Junod spent several days with the man prosecutors have called, "The Boogeyman," and was struck by his mellow demeanor.
Peter Van Sant: Did you ever see on his face, in his eyes, a flash of danger?
Tom Junod: I saw a flash of vacancy. … when you look into the eyes of a shark, they don't look like they hate you. They look like they don't care about you. … And that was Mitchell Gaff.
Gaff was released in 2018, having spent 23 years in civil confinement and in therapy.
Det. Susan Logothetti: There were some professionals there … who did think that they had cured him.
Since then, Logothetti says, Gaff became a Buddhist, married a man and changed his name to Sam Wise Price.

Logothetti said Gaff, now in his 60s, appears to be living a peaceful life. But knowing his violent past, Logothetti shifted her focus back 40 years to the Judy Weaver murder and that DNA breakthrough linking Gaff to her killing. But Logothetti said she now needed a fresh sample to lock him up for good. Logothetti had a plan, that centered on a stick of chewing gum.
Susan Logothetti: I really thought it was a long shot.
The chewing gum sting
It was bold, ingenious and risky.
Peter Van Sant: … the detective usually goes in with a SWAT team. You're now armed with bubble gum. Is that right?
Det. Susan Logothetti: We had gum. Yeah.
Detective Susan Logothetti believed Mitchell Gaff had gotten away with murdering Judy Weaver for almost 40 years. She was going to change that. But first she had to prove it.
Det. Susan Logothetti: This is … items that we used in the gum ruse.
And proving it meant coming up with a plan to collect fresh DNA from her prime suspect —  a plan that involved going undercover to fool Gaff into sampling some chewing gum.
Det. Susan Logothetti: … we were gonna represent a healthy energy gum line that we were launching at Safeway. And it was called —
Peter Van Sant: What was the name of this company?
Det. Susan Logothetti:  —   Energy Gum.
They knew from surveillance that Gaff rarely left the home. So, they decided to go to him.
Det. Susan Logothetti:  I tried to doll up a little bit that day … hoping that would help our chances.
On the morning of Jan. 17, 2024, three detectives, clad in their Zolt Energy T-shirts, knocked on Mitchell Gaff's front door.
Det. Susan Logothetti: And he kinda opens the door a crack … and we start giving our gum excitement spiel.
Det. Susan Logothetti (holding sticks of gum): This is what the gum looked like.
They gave him four unmarked pieces to compare two flavors, watermelon and tropical fruit.
Det. Susan Logothetti: Gaff went with it. He chewed that gum. … it was like he was at a wine tasting … He was talking about the notes of this and hints of that.
Peter Van Sant: … you're sort of a gum sommelier …
Det. Susan Logothetti: Oh, yeah. … I'm writing notes. "Oh, oh." … he got into it.
After each tasting, he would spit the gum into a container held by one of the other detectives.
Det. Susan Logothetti: … I could see the saliva coming out of his mouth, on the gum, in the container.
Peter Van Sant: Exactly what you needed to do a DNA test.
Det. Susan Logothetti: Yes.
After about 30 minutes, they said their goodbyes. Logothetti immediately sent the chewed gum to the crime lab and the results came back in record time.
Det. Susan Logothetti: Everything was confirmed as far as the DNA. There was vaginal swabs … her shirt, the ligatures. …
Peter Van Sant: They all matched to Mitchell Gaff.
Det. Susan Logothetti: They all matched.
Police showed up at The Lucky Lunchbox, Gaff's favorite breakfast spot looking for Sam — Mitchell Gaff's new name.
OFFICER (bodycam): There's some detectives that would like to talk to you down at the police station ...
MITCHELL GAFF: That's interesting.
OFFICER: Yes.
MITCHELL GAFF: Know what it's about?
Det. Susan Logothetti: … he was completely off guard.
OFFICER (bodycam): Uh, before we let you in, we just gotta pat you down for weapons …
OFFICER: I'll hold your sandwich …
MITCHELL GAFF: Do I need, uh, like ID or anything, or?
OFFICER: Eh, no. We know who you are.
When they arrive at the local sheriff's office, Gaff is led up the stairs to the interview room.
Detective Logothetti, whom Gaff didn't seem to recognize as the Zolt gum tester, finally has him where she wants him. She gently broaches the subject at hand.
DET. LOGOTHETTI: Hi. I'm Susie Logothetti …
DET. LOGOTHETTI: … well, you must, you know, wonder why we're here.
MITCHELL GAFF: Oh, yeah. 'Cause right now, yeah, my anxiety and my adrenaline are off the chart. I'm like, what the hell.
DET. LOGOTHETTI: OK. …
MITCHELL GAFF: I'm scared what this is about because holy crap. I've been out – out for a while. I've done nothing and –
Detectives Logothetti and Karen Kowalchyk back off the subject until Gaff can't take the suspense any longer.
MITCHELL GAFF: Why are we here?
DET. LOGOTHETTI: What — um.
MITCHELL GAFF: Why are we here?
Peter Van Sant: You didn't answer that?
Det. Susan Logothetti: No.
Peter Van Sant: OK. You want to hold off?
Det. Susan Logothetti: I did hold off.
Instead, she steers the conversation to the crimes he was convicted of.
Det. Susan Logothetti: I wanted him to talk about how he picked women that he raped.

MITCHELL GAFF (police interview): … I hate to put it in kind of terms, but you ever see the way a cat gets excited by quick movement or something and —  and it —  and it —  it triggers something? It's kind of like that. Something triggered, you know?
He says he never attacked anyone he knew. It was easier that way.
MITCHELL GAFF (police interview): … people were not people, they were objects. It's just a — if I had to admit humanity. If I had to admit a personhood. Would have been harder to do.
He starts talking about the night he sexually abused the teen sisters. Even though one of the sisters says he stalked her after spotting her at a local flower shop, Gaff denies it.
MITCHELL GAFF (police interview): … I didn't have anyone picked out. … I never met them. I never saw them. I did not know …
Logothetti doesn't challenge his account, though she knows from her conversations with the sisters that he is lying.
Det. Susan Logothetti: Mitchell Gaff … while he was raping Myra and Angela told her, "I came here for you, but I couldn't pass up the little treasure that was on the couch," meaning her sister.
He does admit, however, that he would have killed them if Angela hadn't made that escape.
MITCHELL GAFF: I think I had, yeah. I think I had decided that I needed to kill them ...
The detective then circles back to Judy Weaver.
DET. LOGOTHETTI: There is … an incident in — that happened in Everett where, uh, there was a CODIS hit to your DNA. And that's kinda what brought us here today. …
DET. LOGOTHETTI: I mean, do you have any idea what it could have been linked to?
MITCHELL GAFF: No. I committed several rapes, so I don't know.
Mitchell Gaff could see where this conversation was going.
MITCHELL GAFF: I don't know how hard I should try to convict myself.
DET. LOGOTHETTI: What do you mean by that?
MITCHELL GAFF: Well, I obviously do not want to go back to prison for something that happened 40 f****** years ago … I'm just f****** heartbroken.
Det. Susan Logothetti: I gave him a copy of … the warrant.
DET. LOGOTHETTI: … give you a copy of that. …
MITCHELL GAFF: This says "murder."
DET. LOGOTHETTI: Yeah.
Det. Susan Logothetti: And then he went into denial mode. He was like, "what? …Wait a minute, this says murder. I didn't kill anyone."
MITCHELL GAFF: Nobody died. I mean, she was fine.
DET. LOGOTHETTI: … the thing is, is she wasn't fine. Um, I think you know that deep down.
DET. LOGOTHETTI (shows a photo of  Judy Weaver): … there she is.
MITCHELL GAFF: … no idea. I don't know who that is.
DET. LOGOTHETTI: OK. …
DET. LOGOTHETTI: I mean, there's gonna be DNA all over her body.
MITCHELL GAFF: OK. … I don't remember this, but OK. I really don't. Um.
The detectives take DNA swabs.
MITCHELL GAFF: This is really bad. This isn't a rape, this is f****** murder. So, think I should probably have some legal advice.
DET. LOGOTHETTI: … at this point, you're going to be placed under arrest for the murder of Judith Weaver.
The elusive killer undone by a piece of chewing gum.
Detective links Mitchell Gaff to second cold case murder
In January 2025, Detective Susan Logothetti was in the thick of the Judy Weaver murder investigation and preparing for trial. The last thing she expected was this voicemail:
KEN VESEY (voicemail): My name is Ken Vesey. … My wife was murdered … on July 12 of 1980. You guys have stumbled through, done absolutely nothing about it.
Logothetti had never heard the name Ken Vesey before. But that didn't stop her.
Det. Susan Logothetti: I called him immediately … I let him know that … I was unfamiliar with the case. And I — I was hoping you could tell me more.
And so, he did. Ken described in horrifying detail finding his 21-year-old wife Susan Vesey hogtied on the floor of her bedroom, sexually violated and strangled.
Det. Susan Logothetti: I said to him, I need to go get your wife's file, and I'm gonna call you back. … I spent every night reading the file. During that time, I talked to Ken Vesey a lot.

Ken Vesey had lived under a shadow of doubt for more than 40 years as a suspect in his wife's murder. But Logothetti saw the sinister signature of another man in those pages — Mitchell Gaff. It was all there: the strangulation, the electrical cords —
SUSAN LOGOTHETTI (showing evidence): This would have been part of the neck ligature as well …
PETER VAN SANT (holding ligature): So, this went ..  around her neck?
SUSAN LOGOTHETTI: It did.
—   the clothes cut off.
SUSAN LOGOTHETTI: So, these are Susan's jeans that she was wearing the day of …
Det. Susan Logothetti: I called the forensic scientist … and I asked, can I send some evidence up in this 1980 case to be compared with Mitchell Gaff's DNA that we got in the gum ruse?
The answer was yes. Three months later, the report was in her inbox. Mitchell Gaff's DNA was all over the Susan Vesey crime scene.
One of the first calls Logothetti made was to Ken Vesey.
Det. Susan Logothetti: I said, "We got him." I said, "It is – it was Mitchell Gaff."
Prosecutor Craig Matheson, who was preparing for trial in the Judy Weaver case, immediately hit Mitchell Gaff with a second charge: the murder of Susan Vesey.
Prosecutor Craig Matheson: So it was at that point, you know, game on.
But Matheson and his co-counsel Sarah Johnson knew the Vesey case would be tough.

Prosecutor Sarah Johnson: We didn't know if there was anyone alive who had been in the crime scene who could talk about what they saw … But thankfully, Mike Perin was there and he remembered everything.
Mike Perin was a young detective at the time.
Peter Van Sant: What do you see as you enter the apartment? …

Det. Mike Perin: I saw the stuff that makes nightmares. … The person who we later identified as Susan Vesey was on her back … deceased. … sign that she'd been abused sexually and probably tortured also.

Det. Mike Perin (emotional): Whoever did that had a lot of hate … There's some things that humans aren't meant to see. … this is one of those times. It's an image that is, it's as clear now as it was 47 years ago.
Detective Perin later learned that Susan's 2-year-old daughter and 3-month-old son Josh had been found alive in the apartment; Josh on the bed next to where his mother lay dead.
Det. Mike Perin: … just to this day, I thank God that he spared both the children.

Ken Vesey was the one who called 911. At the time, Ken and Susan were getting back together after a brief split. He told detectives he had worked the graveyard shift at a gas station the night of the murder. When he returned to the apartment around 10:30 the morning of July 12, the door was locked. He climbed up the balcony and entered the apartment. He grabbed a knife to cut some of the ligatures off
Det. Mike Perin: He tried to do both mouth-to-mouth and chest compressions. That didn't work. It was way too late.
Peter Van Sant: Your instinct told you what about Ken's story … Was he credible to you?
Det. Mike Perin: He was credible. … he was as upset as any human I've ever seen.
Despite having an airtight alibi – witnesses corroborated he was at work – some detectives on the case continued to believe Ken somehow was the killer.
Paula Keeler: I knew it couldn't be Ken. He loved her. She was the love of his life, you know …
Paula Keeler and Susan Vesey were best friends since childhood.
Paula Keeler: We were soul sisters. … there was a lot of unconditional love between the two of us … she was a woman who loved life and loved people …
And who always longed to be a mother.
Paula Keeler: Susan was very loving, nurturing mother, a very caring mother, very attentive mother …
Susan Vesey turned 21 on July 11, 1980 – the day before she was discovered dead. The two friends, who at the time lived four hours apart, spoke on the phone for the last time on Susan's birthday.
Paula Keeler: We would always say, "I love you," and those were her last words to me.
Decades passed without answers —  45 years of heartbreak before Det. Logothetti made her breakthrough.
Paula Keeler: … she found him. She found him.
Mitchell Gaff pleads guilty
Jackie Brown: … it's changed my life.
Myra: I'm afraid to be alone …
Angela: He knows how much we're hurt. He did it to us.
They were different ages from different walks of life. Some lived.
Peter Van Sant: How lucky do you feel today that you are alive?
Jackie Brown: Very lucky. Very, very lucky.
Some didn't.
Paula Keeler: It's a huge loss.
But they all had one thing in common: a man named Mitchell Gaff.

Prosecutor Sarah Johnson: I would say that Mitchell Gaff is the worst criminal that I've ever come across in my line of work. … Not only the number of crimes that he's committed, but just the scope of how truly terrible all of his crimes were.

Mitchell Gaff was finally slated to stand trial for the murders of Judy Weaver and Susan Vesey in September 2026. But it would never happen. He pleaded guilty five months before it was scheduled to start.
Prosecutor Craig Matheson: I think he saw the strength of the case and —  and knew what was going to happen if we ended up in front of the jury.
One month after his guilty plea, Mitchell Gaff appears in court for sentencing.
Lead prosecutor Craig Matheson makes his case for 61 years behind bars. He begins with the predatory randomness of the murders.
PROSECUTOR MATHESON (in court): Susan Vesey is dead because her front door was unlocked … Judy Weaver made the mistake of arriving home just as the defendant drove by, and she caught his attention …
Matheson spells out his motive: getting pleasure from watching them suffer and die.
PROSECUTOR MATHESON: … to satiate his sexual appetite.
PROSECUTOR MATHESON: He had already taken from them everything that he could have wanted, yet he still decided to kill them both.
Defense Attorney Heather Wolfenbarger counters with what she claims are mitigating circumstances: his age — and his years of therapeutic treatment while incarcerated.
DEFENSE ATTORNEY HEATHER WOLFENBARGER: … and yet we now have this person who is nearly 70 years old …
DEFENSE ATTORNEY WOLFENBARGER: He is simply not the same person that he was then.
DEFENSE ATTORNEY WOLFENBARGER: … we're asking for, we're just—just to impose the statutory, mandatory minimum of 20 years.
Friends and families of Susan Vesey and Judy Weaver then address the human toll.
Judy's nephew, Ernest Bennett, describes seeing his mother – Judy's sister – collapsed in grief after hearing the news.

ERNEST BENNETT(in court): I walk down the hall … to see my mom on the floor on her knees, hands over her head, screaming, yelling, crying, sobbing uncontrollably … That moment is burned into my memory. It has never left me.
Susan Vesey's best friend, Paula Keeler, is still haunted by the details of Susan's violent death.

PAULA KEELER (in court): There are no words that can fully capture what Sue endured in her final moments … Her two young children were present. Her children were present. While they survived physically, their lives and all of our lives were permanently changed.
Susan's son, Josh Vesey – the 3-month-old baby who was in the room when his mother was killed – met us outside the home where the crime occurred and described a different kind of grief.
Josh Vesey: I'm grieving never having any memory of her, right? I never had a mother's unconditional love.
And he watched his father, Ken Vesey, live under the crushing presumption of guilt.
Josh Vesey: … the suspicions were always there … And he was always a suspect … It was probably the worst moment of his life that he had to relive every single day for 46 years.
In a cruel twist, Ken Vesey would never get the chance to face his wife's killer as a vindicated man.
Det. Susan Logothetti: … on July 12 of 2025 … the same day Susan was found, 45 years to the day, Ken Vesey died.
Lastly, Jackie Brown, Mitchell Gaff's first known victim, gives her statement.

JACKIE BROWN (in court): I no longer play music or the radio in my house. I must be able to hear every little noise. … Your Honor, my nightmare occurred 47 years ago, but it seems like yesterday. … I hope your sentence keeps him in prison until his death, Your Honor. Thank you.
Mitchell Gaff, who now goes by the name Sam Price, also addresses the court.
MITCHELL GAFF: I come to you before to take full accountability for my actions, behaviors, and crimes related to the 1980 and 1984 rapes and murders …

But he puts some of the blame on drugs and alcohol and claims he is a changed man.   MITCHELL GAFF: … during the past 40 years in my search for sobriety, sanity, and spirituality, I have spent over 30 years in Buddhist study and Zen meditation.
Paula Keeler: I don't think he's remorseful at all. I think he's just working the court system to get out of it what he could get out of it.

Author Tom Junod —  who spent hours with Gaff in the 1990s reporting that story for GQ Magazine about a therapeutic program for incarcerated sex offenders — believes Gaff conned his therapists into releasing him, while he fundamentally remained the predator he always was.
Tom Junod: … one of the things that you can't forget was that he was cruel. He was a sadist, and he got off on sadism.

Judge Edirin Okoloko sentenced Mitchell Gaff to 50 years in prison —  at his age, a certainty that he will die behind bars. For the first time in 47 years, Jackie Brown believes she can reclaim what she'd lost – maybe even start listening to music again.
Jackie Brown: I will forget it now. I'm determined with the sentence that Judge Okoloko put on Gaff this time …
Paula Keeler hopes Susan Vesey can now shed the tragedy that overshadowed her life.

Paula Keeler: I don't want her to be defined by how she left this world. I want her to be defined by the amazing person that she is, what she stood for in her life and what she lived for while she had the short life that she had.
As the sentencing hearing ends,  Logothetti approaches the man she pursued as relentlessly as he pursued the women he attacked.

Det. Susan Logothetti: It was important for me to handcuff him myself. … He was a —  a predator of women … I just felt like for his victims, a woman should be the one putting the handcuffs on him and walking him into custody where he wasn't gonna be free again.

Produced by Mead Stone  and Liza Finley. Greg Fisher, Cindy Cesare and David Dow are the development producers. Michael Loftus and Gabriella Demirdjian are the field producers. title: Iowa son fights to overturn his father's conviction in mother's murder
summary: Trysten Mullis was 13 when he found his mother Amy Mullis impaled with a corn rake at the family's Iowa farm. In an exclusive interview, the now 21-year-old is speaking out about what he says he witnessed,  determined to overturn his father Todd's murder conviction.
story: Erin Moriarty: Trysten, where are we?
Trysten Mullis: We're at the farm that I grew up on. This is where … me and my brother and sister grew up … these big white buildings here are the hog barns.
Trysten Mullis, along with his younger siblings Taylor and Wyatt, and his parents Todd and Amy, lived on a 400-acre Iowa farm where they grew soybeans and corn and raised pigs.
Trysten Mullis (at the farm): It's a whole family effort to … run a farm this size.
Erin Moriarty: And what are you feeling when you like look out here and --
Trysten Mullis:  Just nostalgia. … it's just kind of peaceful, you know?
What happened at the farm the day Amy Mullis died?
That November morning in 2018, started off routinely. While his sister and brother stayed in the house, Trysten, then 13 years old, was with his parents preparing for a shipment of baby pigs.
Erin Moriarty: This is the office? The shop?
Trysten Mullis: This is the office. Yes.
Trysten showed me inside the hog barn where they were working.
Trysten Mullis (inside the hog barn): Now we're going into the main area of the hog barn. This is where your pigs would actually be in.
Trysten's job that morning was to carry heaters from the front of the barn to each pen. Todd was working on the water supply pipes. Amy was cleaning the lights.

Trysten Mullis (inside the hog barn): What she was doing is she would get on the bucket here and stand up, and she would unscrew it like that (demonstrates). …  Drop it down, get off the bucket, clean it in a separate bucket, and then get back up here and screw them back in.
At one point, Trysten remembers noticing that his mom looked dizzy and unsteady.
Trysten Mullis: She was getting down kind of slow and really grabbing on to the gate … You could kind of see her loopy and swaying a little bit.
Just four days earlier Amy had had a minor medical procedure, and Trysten says he and his dad were concerned. This was her first day back on her feet.
Trysten Mullis: We knew something was not right.

Trysten says his mom agreed to go into the house and rest. But before she left, they asked if she could do one thing on her way: get a pet carrier out of the red shed. Trysten says they needed it later that day to protect some kittens from heavy machinery.
Trysten Mullis: We asked her if she could get it outside of the door.
Trysten says he saw his mom leave.
Trysten Mullis: She walked down the side there.
Erin Moriarty: OK.
Trysten Mullis: And walked out that door … The last time I saw her was through that window, right in the wall there (points to the front end of the barn).
Trysten says he and his dad continued working for about an hour-and-a-half before taking a break.
Trysten Mullis: We noticed that … the pet carrier wasn't outside. So he said, hey, can you go, uh, get the pet carrier out? … We just figured she couldn't get it.
Trysten went to the red shed to get the pet carrier, and that's when he found his mom on the ground with a corn rake in her back.
Trysten Mullis: I was just praying that she was still alive.
Trysten yelled for his dad, and they got Amy into the truck —  calling 911 as they rushed to the hospital.
911 OPERATOR: Delaware County 911. What's the address of your emergency?
TODD MULLIS (to Trysten): Is she breathing?
TODD MULLIS: I just grabbed her and threw her in the truck. My son's holding her.
911 OPERATOR: OK, you're headed to the hospital and she's in your vehicle?
Erin Moriarty: How did you hear that your mom didn't make it?
Trysten Mullis: Dad walked in the room and he had tears in his eyes … and told us that mom had passed away.
Amy's mother Peggy, her brother Jeff and her stepfather Randy are still coming to terms with what happened that day.
Peggy Munson: Your heart stops.
Jeff Fuller: She was my best friend … growing up … Amy was a very vibrant person. She had a big personality.
Randy Munson: She was always concerned about other people, about her family, about her children.
Trysten says that he and his father assumed his mother's death had been a horrible accident; that she had just fallen on the rake. But less than a year later, Todd was on trial for her murder.

Even though Todd and Trysten maintained that Amy's death was an accident, the state medical examiner, Dr. Kelly Kruse, said it was a homicide. She found a large bruise on the side of Amy's jaw and scrapes and bruises on Amy's knuckles — possible signs of a — noted that while Amy had six puncture wounds on her back, the corn rake only had four tines.
DR. KELLY KRUSE (testifying at trial): There were two different directions of the six puncture wounds. …
PROSECUTOR MAUREEN HUGHES: And what do those different directions indicate to you?
DR. KELLY KRUSE: To me they indicate that she would have to be impaled with the rake at least twice. … possibly three times.

Dr. Kruse determined that Amy's injuries had to have been caused by someone striking her with the rake. Iowa Division of Criminal Investigation special agent Jon Turbett, now retired, was called in to help local law enforcement.
Jon Turbett: I'm thinking at some point Todd and Amy end up in that red barn, and Todd attacks Amy … and … she's hit two or three times with a corn rake.
And he says Todd had a motive.
Jon Turbett: We learn that the marriage … is not … maybe what it would look like on the outside … There were things boiling underneath.
Amy was having an affair, and according to her brother Jeff, she wasn't happy and planned to leave Todd.
Jeff Fuller: Her words to me were, "Todd's gonna flip out."
Erin Moriarty: And what did that mean to you? What did flip out mean to you?
Jeff Fuller: To me, that meant that he would … not go quietly, he would not give up half of … his land … in a divorce.
Jon Turbett: And that becomes … a big part of his motive of killing Amy.
And according to her friend Patricia Christopherson, Amy was afraid of Todd.
PATRICIA CHRISTOPHERSON (testifying at trial): I asked her why she stayed and she said she was scared of Todd and if he found out about, um, wanting a divorce or an affair, that he would kill her.
Investigators say Google searches found on Todd's iPad show that not only did he think about killing his wife, he planned it in advance.
Jon Turbett: You see searches on … unfaithful wives … and killing cheating wives at different points in history.
According to prosecutors, Todd's plan was to send Amy to the red shed that morning and then ambush and kill her, But that wasn't all.
PROSECUTOR MAUREEN HUGHES (at trial): He sent his 13-year-old son to go and find his mother, who he had just slaughtered.
When Todd testified, he told the jury he never did those damning Google searches, that he did not know his wife was having an affair, and that he did not kill her.
DEFENSE ATTORNEY GERALD FEUERHELM (at trial): Todd … did you ambush your wife, Amy, in that shed that day and brutally beat her and chop — chop her up with that corn fork?
TODD MULLIS: No, I did not.

Since Trysten was the only other person working on the farm that day, his testimony was crucial. He initially told police that he had been with his dad all morning — essentially providing an alibi for his father. Trysten later added that he did leave his dad's side twice to get a drink of water and that he briefly lost sight of him. Because he was a minor, Trysten wasn't shown on camera.
PROSECUTOR (at trial): Do you know exactly how long your dad wasn't in your sight?
TRYSTEN MULLIS: No.
PROSECUTOR: … Trysten, would it be accurate to say that you don't know how much time you were away from your dad ... when you were working in the hog barn?
TRYSTEN MULLIS: Yes.
And according to prosecutors, that gave Todd the time to kill Amy. But Trysten says he was pressured to testify the way he did — pressured by Amy's stepfather.
What Trysten Mullis wants a jury to know about what happened the day his mother died
Erin Moriarty: How would you describe the last eight years?
Trysten Mullis: Hell. I would say hell.

Trysten Mullis says his testimony at his father's murder trial didn't tell the whole story and if he could do it all over again, here's what he would want the jury to know about how long it took to get a drink of water that day.
Trysten Mullis: … I said I don't know how much time. I wasn't saying it could have been 20 minutes or whatever … It was a matter of seconds.
All he had to do, he says, was walk around a corner at the front of the barn.
Trysten Mullis: Right here is the hose that I drank out of that day.
Erin Moriarty: And so where do you drink out of it, like right here?
Trysten Mullis (drinks from the hose): Right out of the nozzle right here.
Erin Moriarty: You didn't do anything else in here?
Trysten Mullis: Nope. And then you walk right back in.
And that, he says, is just not enough time for his father to leave, kill his mother and come back. There were two ways Todd could have gone. Either through a door at the front of the barn —
Erin Moriarty:  If he went that way.
Trysten Mullis: He would walk right past me.
Erin Moriarty: You would have seen him.
Trysten Mullis: I would have seen him and I would have heard him.
Erin Moriarty: So what's the only other way he could have gone out?
Trysten Mullis: The only other way he could have gone out is to the end of the barn, all the way down at the end there.
Erin Moriarty: Oh, I see the door —
Trysten Mullis: See the door?
Erin Moriarty:  —  right down there.
Trysten Mullis: Yep.
Erin Moriarty: Then to get to the shed, how would he have to do that?
Trysten Mullis: would have to run all the way across the barn and then run all the way down.
Then —
Trysten Mullis: He'd have to jump the gate, run through the trees, go into the barn, do whatever, and run all the way back.
The round trip would have been about the length of four football fields.
Trysten Mullis: Come through the door, get back to the spot. Not be out of breath, not be panicked, not be, you know, frightened in any way, shape or form.
Erin Moriarty: … did your dad seem to be disheveled when — any time when you saw him there or out of breath or —
Trysten Mullis: Absolutely not.
For a young boy, it was a lot to handle.
Trysten Mullis: I've had to grow up really fast … going from a 13-year-old kid now taking care of two … younger siblings … trying to lead them.
When his father was arrested for the murder of his mother, Trysten, his sister Taylor, then 11, and brother Wyatt, 9, went to live with Amy's family three hours away.
Peggy Munson (emotional): I'd always promised her that I would look after her children. … But little did I know they would be living with us.
Amy's mom Peggy.
Peggy Munson: It was hard for us too, because we were still grieving.

It was painful all around. The kids had to adjust to a new town and a new school. But for Trysten, there was no adjusting to the fact that he was living with family that he says believed his father was a killer.

Trysten Mullis: And I — to this day I've tried to get them to change their mind … and they still don't believe that he's innocent. … it's caused a lot of tension in that side of the family because of what they believe and what I believe.

So at 17, with the help of a lawyer, Trysten took action. He signed an affidavit accusing Amy's stepfather Randy and an attorney hired by Amy's family of pressuring him on how to testify at trial if asked about how long his father was out of his sight:

They said that if I did not answer the question with "I don't know" to the question then I would get in trouble for my mom's death and be sent to a jail for kids called juvenile detention and that I would be taken out of school and away from my friends.
Erin Moriarty: As you know, Randy … He said in his affidavit that that you had pressured him …
Randy Munson: Yeah. No, just tell the truth. …
Erin Moriarty: Was that hard to read?
Peggy Munson: Yes.
Randy Munson: Yes, it is.

Peggy Munson: Very much so. Because that's the last thing that we did with those kids is tell them to say anything — they speak their own mind … The truth is what we want them to say. Yeah, that was hard, very hard.
Today, Trysten does not want to talk about his affidavit.
Trysten Mullis: it's kind of a sensitive area.

But when he rewinds back through the murder trial, all he can see are mistakes and missed opportunities to prove that his mother's death was accidental — starting with his father's defense counsel. In a letter to his lawyer written from jail before the trial, Todd asked, "is there any 'expert' that could verify possibility of it being accident." In another, Todd made a rudimentary sketch of how he thought it happened.
But when the trial began Todd's defense attorney Gerald Feuerhelm didn't even argue it was an accident. He told the jury that Amy was murdered.
DFENSE ATORNEY GERALD FEURHELM (at trial): Amy Mullis was viciously and deliberately murdered …
... Just not by Todd. Todd's sister Lynne and brother Mike watched on helplessly.
Mike Mullis: Well, when the – when the defense comes out and says, well, we know this was a murder, and but Todd didn't do it. Well, that was an opening statement, my God –
Lynne White: Where did this come from? It made no sense.
When "48 Hours" reached out to Feuerhelm, he declined our request to be interviewed but he has said that he never considered an accidental death for Todd's defense.
Dina Nesheiwat: Nobody got to hear anything — any evidence of accidents.

Now Todd's family is leaning on new lawyers who hope to overturn his murder conviction. Brother and sister Daniel and Dina Nesheiwat have taken over the case. Years earlier, the Nesheiwats were consultants for "48 Hours" when we covered Todd's murder trial. And when they dug into the case, they too concluded that Todd didn't have enough time to kill Amy. Daniel did the leg work himself.

Daniel Nesheiwat: I literally ran the distance that the prosecution was accusing Todd of — of doing so he could have committed this alleged murder. And being there and seeing it, it's impossible. It's a — quite a distance … there's no way it could have been done just on that fact. … And — and at that point, I was 100 percent convinced.
How did the corn rake end up in Amy Mullis' back?
Convinced that Todd Mullis had not murdered his wife, his new attorneys Dina and Daniel Nesheiwat did what Todd said he had wanted all along.
Erin Moriarty: What is this here?
Dr. Jennifer Hammers: So this is the shed. This is where Amy was actually found.

They hired experts, including Forensic Pathologist Dr. Jennifer Hammers – a former New York City and Boston medical examiner — and Dr. Valentina Ngai, a biomechanical engineer. And after going to the scene, examining the evidence and doing tests of their own, they both say Amy was not murdered that day.
Dr. Jennifer Hammers: This does not appear to be a homicide to me. …

At trial the state medical examiner testified that Amy had that bruise on her jaw and scrapes and bruises on her knuckles. But if Amy had been hit in the face by Todd, Hammers says, there also would've been swelling.
Dr. Jennifer Hammers: The area isn't swollen. … if this area is impacted in, let's say, a physical altercation, we very often see pretty quick bruising … swelling of that area

As for the scrapes and bruises on Amy's knuckles,  Hammers suggests that those injuries could have come from cleaning those glass light fixtures that Amy was doing earlier that day. As Trysten showed me, they were very narrow.
Erin Moriarty (in the hog barn holding glass fixture): Your mom was cleaning this out by —
Trysten Mullis: Hand.
Erin Moriarty (putting her hand inside the fixture): This is hard.
Trysten Mullis: Mm-hmm.
Erin Moriarty: I don't have big hands.
Trysten Mullis: Mm-hmm.
But the most crucial question for these experts is how the corn rake ended up in Amy's back.
Erin Moriarty: At trial, basically everyone said four tines, six injuries. Simple math. Murder. …
Dr. Valentina Ngai: That is not right.
Dr. Jennifer Hammers: That's incorrect.

Using the state medical examiner's notes, Hammers drew an approximate diagram of the wounds, labeling them A through F. And then she and Ngai examined the direction of each wound. They, like the state medical examiner, say the wounds go in two different directions.
Dr. Valentina Ngai: If you look at A, B, C, D … these wounds travel through the body almost perpendicular …. and E and F are sharply upward.
But unlike the state medical examiner, they don't think the wounds came from Todd striking her with the rake multiple times.
Dr. Valentina Ngai: That scenario of … swinging and re-swinging does not fit … it does not match the physical evidence.
Dr. Valentina Ngai: … if you swing it, the entry points are much more steep. … swinging with these tines causes a much steeper entry point and would not generate these wound trajectories.
So, if someone didn't strike Amy with the corn rake, how did she end up with six puncture wounds in her back?
Erin Moriarty: Are you trying to reconstruct what must have happened to Amy?
Dr. Valentina Ngai: Yes.
They concluded that Amy accidentally fell on the rake and helped to create an animation. After initially falling on the rake, Amy, they say, struggled to free herself from it.
Dr. Jennifer Hammers: None of those injuries are gonna immediately incapacitate her. So she would be able to move, to … try to remove it from her body.
And in trying to remove it from her body, they say, she wounded herself further.
Erin Moriarty: So, what you're saying is that when Amy tried to get the corn rake out of her back … she inadvertently caused greater injury?
Dr. Jennifer Hammers: Yes.
Here's their opinion of what happened. When Amy fell, three of the four tines pierced her coat and her back, creating three puncture wounds.  Hammers and Ngai say Amy then tried to get up.

Dr. Valentina Ngai: She can't roll to her left, otherwise she rolls over top of the rake. … She can't sit upright because the rake handle is too long and it hits the ground … The only way for her to be able to get up is to roll to her right.

As she struggled, they say, she managed to free one tine from her back, but it still stayed under her coat. They say she fell again, causing the fourth puncture wound. Then Amy once again tried to free herself from the rake.
Dr. Valentina Ngai: She gets up to her knees and grabs the rake handle.

Still trying to break free, Hammers and Ngai say that Amy inadvertently turned the rake, changing the direction of the tines. They say she fell again, causing the fifth and sixth puncture wounds while the tines were pointing upward.
Dr. Valentina Ngai: … falling back onto those last two tines explains … that upward internal trajectory.

Doctors Hammers and Ngai say the clearest proof that Amy's death could not have been caused by someone swinging the rake is the coat that Amy was wearing that day. A photo of the inside of the coat, shown above, taken at autopsy— but never shown at trial — the four arrows indicate where the medical examiner saw holes in the coat.
Dr. Valentina Ngai: Is a extremely important piece of evidence. … because it indicates that the clothing has less holes than the number of holes in her body. …
Erin Moriarty: And why is that so significant?

Dr. Valentina Ngai: He was convicted on swinging this rake multiple times into her body. How do you swing a four-tine implement multiple times and have less holes in the outer clothes and more holes in the body? That is illogical.

And they think they know why Amy fell in the first place. Dr. Hammers discovered a potential clue in Amy's medical records – something the medical examiner later said she didn't look at. Not only did Amy have that medical procedure a few days earlier —
Dr. Jennifer Hammers: … she had three medications, all of which can cause some sort of dizziness … or sleepiness.

Remember, Trysten had said his mother appeared dizzy and unsteady. As part of their work, Hammers and Ngai walked through the farm. They say that the layout of the red shed likely contributed to the accident.
Dr. Jennifer Hammers: It's very dark. It's very narrow … there's a lot of things in there.

To get the pet carrier, Amy had to walk down one narrow pathway, turn right, and then walk down another. Police photos from that day show the pet carrier sticking out. And Ngai and Hammers noticed something else in those photos – on the ground there were two pieces of farm equipment, called augers, that look like giant drill bits.
Dr. Jennifer Hammers: With the pet carrier being partially pulled out … it seems most likely that she was starting to pull that out.
Dr. Valentina Ngai: The barn being dark …. the augers at your feet, a tripping hazard, falling backwards. … this is the most likely plausible scenario.
For Trysten and the Mullis family, the experts' conclusion is what they'd been waiting for.
Lynne White: Finally, Todd's explanation's right here. … they proved it … science doesn't lie.  … it was a farm accident. Simple as that.
Trysten Mullis: I felt like we had our answer.
But when Todd's new attorneys get the chance to present this information to a judge, would it be enough?
Todd Mullis seeks new trial
Determined to prove that Amy Mullis' death was an accident —
Dina Nesheiwat: … you can't argue with the science. You can't argue with the biomechanical engineers.

— they need to convince an Iowa judge in this courtroom that Todd's defense counsel who never investigated the possibility of an accidental death was ineffective, and that if the evidence they have collected now had been presented at his original trial, there might have been a different result. If they can do that, they hope to win Todd a new trial. On that day in court, Todd saw his children for the first time in six years.
Trysten Mullis: I broke down. I — I broke down. Just to see his face like tore me apart. … I just wanted to jump over the rail and hug him, tell him I loved him.
The Nesheiwats— along with a team of lawyers from both the Iowa Wrongful Conviction Unit and the Exoneration Project —are working pro bono to challenge Todd's murder conviction.
Tara Thompson: Nobody listened to Todd at trial … the outcome of his trial would've been different if the jury had heard everything that the court is gonna hear over the course of this trial.
At his murder trial, the prosecution argued that Amy's affair was the reason Todd killed her. But the Nesheiwats say there's no clear evidence that Todd had any idea that his marriage was at risk.
Dina Nesheiwat: … she was having an affair at that time, um, unbeknownst to Todd. … but never took any action to actually take the steps to leaving.
And in the month before she died, says Dina Nesheiwat, there were affectionate texts between them.
Dina Nesheiwat: There's messages where they're saying I love you back and forth. …
But what about that conversation that Amy's friend said they had about being afraid Todd would kill her?

Dina Nesheiwat: I think they were … for lack of better words, kind of throwaway … statements … Just like if I said it, you know, "my husband's gonna kill me if I'm home late," you know or things of that nature. … if she believed he was going to kill her … she would have done something different, and she didn't. She stayed.
As for those Google searches discovered on Todd Mullis' iPad — searches about cheating and killing unfaithful women — which Todd denied making but the prosecution said proved premeditation —
Erin Moriarty: How do you explain the Google searches? … "what happens to cheaters in history?" "Killing unfaithful women." That looks bad.
Dina Nesheiwat: Yes. On their face, they do look bad. … In isolation, they do look bad.
Dina Nesheiwat says that all those searches were made before Amy even began her affair — and she says that many of the searches were about history.
Dina Nesheiwat: But if you follow the search sequence it goes into different cultures.
Including one that asked: "what happened to cheating spouses in historic Aztec tribe"
Dina Nesheiwat: … The state told the jury that all of the searches from Todd Mullis' Gmail account were done on the iPad, but that's not the case.
Todd's Google account was used on more than just his iPad, including Amy's phone and a family laptop, so Nesheiwat says anyone in the Mullis home could have done those searches.
Dina Nesheiwat: We don't know who did the search. ...

But for Todd's attorneys, it's not enough to raise questions about the circumstantial evidence against Todd Mullis. Success at this hearing hinges on the new defense witnesses. They testified without using the animation. It was not yet ready.
ATTORNEY TARA THOMPSON (in court): Did you reach an opinion in this case, Dr. Hammers, about how you would classify the manner of Ms. Mullis' death?
DR. JENNIFER HAMMERS: I did.
ATTORNEY TARA THOMPSON: And what is your conclusion after consideration of all of the background evidence and the evaluation of the hypotheses that you considered in this case?
DR. JENNIFER HAMMERS: My opinion is that the manner of death is best classified as an accident.
ATTORNEY TARA THOMPSON: Good afternoon, Dr. Ngai.
DR. VALENTINA NGAI: Good afternoon.

ATTORNEY TARA THOMPSON: During your investigation, did you come across any physical evidence that did not fit with this hypothesis of Ms. Mullis falling onto the rake in the way that you've described?
DR. VALENTINA NGAI:  No. Every single piece of physical evidence supported this hypothesis.
ATTORNEY TARA THOMPSON: And are these opinions that you could have — you or someone else in the biomechanical field could have offered back in 2019 based on the state of the science then?
DR. VALENTINA NGAI: Yes.

Given the evidence, Hammers and Ngai said that Amy's injuries could only be the result of an accidental fall. That contradicts Dr. Kelly Kruse, the state medical examiner, who declined to speak with "48 Hours."

ATTORNEY TARA THOMPSON: Is it true that at the time of Ms. Mullis' autopsy, that because you could not envision a circumstance in which Ms. Mullis sustained these injuries, other than … someone impaling her with the corn rake, that that is the reason you determined that this was a homicide?
DR. KELLY KRUSE: There is no other way. Yes.
ASSISTANT ATTORNEY GENERAL SCOTT BROWN: Any of those, um, opinions or characterizations have those changed for you at all over this course of time?
DR. KELLY KRUSE: No.
ASSISTANT ATTORNEY GENERAL SCOTT BROWN: OK. You've reviewed a report that has essentially criticized your findings in this case, correct?
DR. KELLY KRUSE: Yes.
ASSISTANT ATTORNEY GENERAL SCOTT BROWN: And has that review caused you to change any of the opinions that you've given in this case?
DR. KELLY KRUSE: No.

Lawyers for the state questioned Kruse and did not bring any new witnesses to dispute the evidence presented by Hammers and Ngai. But they argued at the end of the hearing that Todd Mullis' murder conviction should not be overturned.
ASSISTANT ATTORNEY GENERAL THOMAS BAKKE (in court): The state submits that Mr. Mullis has not met his burden of proof on any of his claims. We ask the court to deny his application in its entirety.
Trysten did not testify at the hearing but a deposition, in which he described being pressured, was submitted. He was a fixture in court throughout – sitting right behind his father.
Erin Moriarty: …You were there every day.

Trysten Mullis: Every single day. I mean, why wouldn't I be there every single day … I know he's innocent. And for the judge to see that … Well, his son is the one sitting behind him the whole time, you know.

TARA THOMPSON (in court): … Mr. Mullis has established there is at least a reasonable likelihood that the outcome of this trial would've been different with the overwhelming evidence that the Court has seen, this is evidence of an innocent man. This is evidence of a man that deserves a new trial, and a trial where he can have his day in court.
And with closing arguments said and done, Trysten felt confident.
Trysten Mullis: I thought he was gonna walk out of the courtroom that day after the experts testified. I thought they were gonna let him walk right out of there, to be honest with you.
Now they wait.
Trysten Mullis' Fight Continues
Trysten Mullis: I thought it was going to be a quick, yeah, this is obvious. He needs a new trial. This is completely unfair.
It wasn't quick.
Daniel Nesheiwat: … every day seems like a month. And then when those days turn into months, turn into over a year … It's very tolling on everyone involved.
The hearing lasted six days but it would take nearly 15 months before Judge Laura Parrish made her decision.
Dina Nesheiwat: She denied Todd relief and getting a new trial.

Everything Todd's new lawyers argued was rejected. The judge ruled that "Todd Mullis received a fair trial represented by competent counsel." What's more, she placed blame on Todd himself. Dina Nesheiwat described the judge's ruling.
Dina Nesheiwat: … the … gist of it was Todd wanted to go to trial, so the attorney didn't have enough time to investigate … he knew he was going without … an expert. … which we disagree with.

The judge also said the jury found Dr. Kruse, the state medical examiner, "credible" and that her "testimony was consistent with the other evidence they relied on." But as for the arguments at the heart of the Nesheiwat's case, the work they did that shows that Amy Mullis died as a result of an accident, Judge Parrish said little.
Dina Nesheiwat: … she summarized the science, but she didn't analyze the science …
Erin Moriarty: If the jury had heard the science, do you think that would have made a difference at trial?
Daniel Nesheiwat: Absolutely.
Dina Nesheiwat: Todd would not be in prison right now if a jury heard the evidence that we have here or saw that animation.
The decision was devastating to Trysten and the rest of the Mullis family who had been so hopeful.
Mike Mullis: We went through all the work … to prove all this.
Lynne White: To prove this.
Mike Mullis: And then –
Lynne White: Yeah, basically have it dismissed.
Mike Mullis: Disregarded basically.
Erin Moriarty: How frustrated is your family?
Mike Mullis: Very frustrated.
Lynne White: Very frustrated.
Trysten Mullis: ... I was dumbfounded that a — a judge could look at that and decide that.
Dina Nesheiwat had to break the news to Todd.
Dina Nesheiwat: …he was just crushed. …sucked the air right out of him. Just couldn't believe it. … what else do they want? What else do they need?
Dina Nesheiwat: … science doesn't pick sides.
Still, there are plenty of people who already have, and believe that Judge Parrish and the jury at Todd's trial got it right.
Erin Moriarty: Is there any chance in your mind that this could have been an accident? …

Jon Turbett: No. I think Todd Mullis killed Amy Mullis … the evidence was put before and tested by juries and appellate, you know, judges. And, um, I absolutely believe we got the right outcome on that.
Jeff Fuller: … if you look at the evidence, there was no way that it was an accident.
Amy's brother Jeff said he found the defense experts conclusion far-fetched.
Jeff Fuller: … it seemed to me that they were trying to retry the case … with some alternate facts and alternate theories. … it seemed almost nonsensical, some of the things that were being said.
Amy's brother, mother and stepfather are hoping the judge's decision will finally shift the focus from Todd and put it back on Amy.
Peggy Munson: There's a hole in our lives, but we know she's up there in Heaven looking down on us.
Erin Moriarty: What's the most important thing that you want people to know about Amy?
Jeff Fuller: Um, the number one thing is how much she loved her kids. And how great of a mom she was.
Randy Munson: … we know how we feel about losing her, but I can't imagine how they feel.
Erin Moriarty: So what do you do now?

Dina Nesheiwat: We keep fighting. We have an appeal to go to next and we're just going to keep fighting. … the science is still on the record just because she didn't analyze it or agree with it or — it's still there, still on the record. So we're going to ask an appellate court to hear it now.
Erin Moriarty: You're not giving up.
Lynne White: No.
Mike Mullis: Absolutely not.
Erin Moriarty: Why not?
Mike Mullis: 'Cause we know he's innocent.
Trysten Mullis: I lost both of my parents at 13. …
Trysten told us he's not giving up either. He often thinks of his mom and is determined to get justice for his father.
Erin Moriarty: What keeps you going?
Trysten Mullis: Prayer, prayer and faith that one day this will all be set straight …
Erin Moriarty: If he were sitting here right now, what would you say to your dad?
Trysten Mullis: I love you and I'm — I'm fighting every day for you. I'm fighting to get you home.

title: Alligator kills 71-year-old man fishing at pond in Florida
summary: The man was dragged into a pond and killed by the alligator, according to authorities.
story: A 71-year-old man fishing at a pond in Winter Garden, Florida, on Friday was dragged into the water and killed by a nearly 12-foot alligator, according to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.
The victim was identified as Steve Hamilton, according to Florida wildlife officials.

The attack happened at about 5 p.m. in Dr. Bradford Memorial Park, which has several small ponds connected to the larger Lake Apopka. The location is well known for its alligators. The park even has a crossing called Gator Bridge.
"Lake Apopka has tons of alligators in it, so that's not uncommon to see alligators in this part of town at all," Winter Garden Police Capt. Michael Mason told reporters Friday night.
The fisherman was on shore at the time of the attack and pulled into the water, Mason said. An 11-foot, 8-inch alligator was trapped and removed from the scene, the FWC said.
"Always be aware of your surroundings, always be safe. Local wildlife, respect it, keep your distance. It looks like it's docile, it looks like your Florida emblem, but it can be dangerous."

Hamilton is the second person to be killed by an alligator in Florida this year. Brittany Clark, 31, was killed in June while swimming in Little Big Econ State Forest near Orlando. Her boyfriend and friends tried to save her but she was later pronounced dead. On the 911 call, someone is heard saying she lost one arm and nearly the second and was "losing a lot of blood."
"It's bad," her boyfriend says in the 911 call. "It's really bad. Please hurry."

Alligator attacks in Florida are still fairly rare, despite there being hundreds of thousands of the animals in the state. Outside of 2022, when there were 23 attacks on humans, the total number of attacks usually hovers around a dozen each year, according to the FWC.

There were 13 attacks last year in Florida, including eight major attacks, two of which were fatal, according to the data. There have been 32 fatal alligator attacks in Florida since they began keeping track in 1948. There have never been more than three fatal attacks in a year.

The two fatal attacks in 2025 included Cynthia Diekema, 61, who was attacked while canoeing in Polk County in May; and Deborah Herndon, 73, who was found dead in December at a residential pond in Pinellas County.

title: Vance says admin. must take action when ICE agents "screw up"
summary: Vice President JD Vance acknowledged that there are some federal immigration officers "who really screw up."
story: Washington — Vice President JD Vance acknowledged that there are some federal immigration officers "who really screw up" and said the Trump administration has a responsibility to take action against those who do.

Vance sat down with "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil for a one-hour town hall in Michigan, which aired Saturday. Michigan is home to one of the closely watched Senate races between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.
During an exchange about immigration, Vance drew comparisons between law enforcement officers and members of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE.

"Most of them are amazing people who are patriots and they wanna do a good job protecting their country. Sometimes you have some people who make mistakes. Sometimes you have some people who really screw up," Vance said. "And obviously, we have a responsibility to prosecute, investigate when people do screw up."

Dokoupil pressed the vice president on some of those instances, noting that in some cases, "people talk about them before they're investigated," and he asked Vance about the biggest mistakes involving ICE's immigration actions. Vance declined to single out any incidents but said the Trump administration has responded when officers have been accused of misconduct.

"There are a number of cases where we've investigated and either provided further training, or sometimes even provided disciplinary situations within ICE," the vice president said. "We don't always advertise that stuff, as you know, Tony, because we believe that people have to be judged in a court of law and through a normal investigatory process."

Since the Trump administration has ramped up immigration enforcement actions as part of President Trump's immigration crackdown, officers with ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Protection have come under criticism for their use-of-force practices.

Two Americans, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were shot and killed by immigration authorities during protests in Minnesota earlier this year. The ICE officer who fatally shot Good, Jonathan Ross, was placed on administrative leave shortly after the shooting. In May, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul questioned whether Ross had been reassigned to her state. The Department of Homeland Security declined to say at the time where Ross was working.
No criminal charges have been filed in either case. The Justice Department opened an investigation into Pretti's shooting earlier this year.
There have since been a series of incidents involving immigration officers during targeted enforcement operations.
An ICE officer in May fatally shot a 25-year-old Colombian man in his car in Maine in July, and in September, an immigration officer shot a Venezuelan man in the back in Austin, Texas.

Earlier this month, ICE agents shot a man in New York during a targeted enforcement operation, striking him in the neck. The agents were trying to arrest the man, Oscar Belgal, who is from the Dominican Republic, with a 5-year-old boy in the back seat.
Then, a vehicle driven by ICE agents hit and injured a man near Houston.

title: Trudy weakens to Category 1 storm after dumping heavy rain on Mexico
summary: Trudy was expected to turn toward the west-northwest Sunday night into Monday, taking it away from Mexico's coast and south of the Baja California Peninsula on Monday and Tuesday.
story: Hurricane Trudy brought heavy rain and powerful winds to parts of Mexico's Pacific coast on Sunday, impacting sections of the country's western and southwestern states that were already targeted by Hurricane Simon last week.

By Sunday night, all hurricane watches and warnings for Mexico's coast had expired. The National Hurricane Center, which is based in Miami, had urged people in coastal regions of Michoacán, Colima and Jalisco to prepare for potentially life-threatening flooding and mudslides as a result of impending rain.

As of the hurricane center's latest update, issued Sunday night, Trudy had maximum sustained winds of 80 mph, making it a Category 1 hurricane. The storm had strengthened into a major Category 3 hurricane as it tracked toward Mexico late last week, but it has since weakened. Further rapid weakening was expected Sunday night into Monday, with the possibility of the storm being downgraded to a post-tropical depression by Tuesday night.
On Sunday, Trudy was about 130 miles west-southwest of Cabo Corrientes, Mexico, and moving northwest at 7 mph.
Trudy's center was expected to turn toward the west-northwest Sunday night into Monday, taking it away from Mexico's coast and south of the Baja California Peninsula on Monday and Tuesday.

The Mexican Navy urged mariners and coastal residents to exercise extreme caution earlier Sunday because of high waves, heavy rain and the risk of rising rivers, flooding and landslides in vulnerable areas.
Colima authorities said the risks remained low, but warned that heavy rainfall could cause damage because the ground was already saturated by successive storms along the Pacific coast.

Trudy was expected to bring 4 to 8 inches of rain through the weekend, with isolated totals of around 12 inches along and near the coast in Michoacán, Colima and Jalisco. The hurricane center said areas with steep terrain were particularly vulnerable to serious flooding and mudslides.
Other Pacific storms

Also in the Pacific, Typhoon Champi was moving into the Philippine Sea after passing close to Guam 's southern tip, packing sustained winds of 140 mph. By late Sunday, it was 345 miles west of Guam and moving west-northwest at 14 mph, according to the U.S. National Weather Service.

Champi was forecast to weaken before potentially strengthening into a Category 5 typhoon by Monday evening, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, part of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, said.
All tropical cyclone watches and warnings for Guam, Rota, Tinian and Saipan had been canceled.
The governors of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands requested emergency disaster declarations on Friday.

On Saturday, President Trump approved an emergency declaration for Guam authorizing FEMA to coordinate all federal disaster relief efforts. FEMA announced that federal disaster assistance was available for the territory of Guam to supplement local response efforts following Typhoon Champi.
Airports, harbors and some health facilities in the territories were closed. Relief supplies were unlikely to reach the islands for three to five days, according to Saturday updates from FEMA.
The territories are still recovering from super typhoons Sinlaku and Bavi, which struck in April and July, respectively.

title: Pope Leo says he will resume activities after cancer surgery
summary: Pope Leo XIV​ thanked thousands of faithful in St. Peter's Square on Sunday, one day after being discharged from the hospital for cancer surgery.
story: Pope Leo XIV thanked thousands of faithful in St. Peter's Square on Sunday for their prayers while he was hospitalized for an operation to remove a malignant tumor, and said he plans to gradually return to his usual duties.

The crowd erupted in cheers when the pontiff showed himself in the window overlooking the square, where a week ago on the same occasion of the traditional Angelus blessing he revealed that a nodule had been located on his lung, and that it would be surgically removed.

''Now that this delicate phase is behind me, I will gradually resume my activities, always with God's help and your prayers," Leo said, his voice sounding strong four days after the lower lobe of his right lung was removed.
"This experience has made me feel particularly close to all those who are living with illness or infirmity," the pope said.
He told the crowd that he had ''truly felt your support,'' and expressed ''particular gratitude to the doctors, nurses and all the staff at Gemelli Hospital," where he was treated.
The pope paused for a moment and waved to the crowd before retreating into his apartment in the Apostolic Palace.
A delegation from Africa in Rome for a congress danced and ululated after the pope's blessing.
''He was always in our prayers when he was sick, and we are happy to see him today,″ said Alain Kalembu of the Democratic Republic of Congo. ″This is an expression of our joy.″

The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

He told a reporter in English that he was doing ''much better'' as he drove away from Rome's Gemelli Hospital to return to the Vatican, after a shorter hospital stay than had initially been anticipated. He was discharged Saturday after the four-day stay. No information about his prognosis has been publicly shared.

"I don't believe it, because he was just operated on the other day," said Cosimo Mastrocinque, a retired factory worker visiting the Vatican from the southern region of Puglia. "It is a miracle that he recovered already."

American tourists were especially eager to pray alongside the first pope born in the United States. Marla Marsala of Michigan was supposed to attend a Mass with the pope last week that was canceled due to his hospitalization.

''I am just happy that we are praying with him today instead of for him, like we were before,'' Marsala said. "It was a tough week for all of the people who love him, which are many. He seems like a very strong soul. So I think he will pull through and fight it, and succeed and keep doing the wonderful work he is doing.''
Claire Holland from Jacksonville, Florida, said she felt "very blessed" to be present for the pope's return to his flock.

"I'm so happy that he has recovered so quickly. I think there have been millions and millions of prayers. And he is a strong, determined man, and I am so happy that he is feeling well enough to do this," Holland said.

Leo's next major engagement is an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, including a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes. His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News on Saturday that "there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place."
"The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery," Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery "in another 10 days or so."

Histological testing of the tumor and related lymph nodes was underway. The results, along with details of the tumor's molecular and genetic makeup, will help doctors determine whether the pope needs additional treatment. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted oral therapy based on the tumor's genetic characteristics.
